sections.h: FOREWORD REPORT MADE TO THE COMMITTEE ON HISTORICAL AND SCIENTIFIC WORKS
p: Per m. BERTHELOT ON THE COLLECTION OF THE ALCHIMICAL GREEK MANUSCRITS AND ON THE USE OF THEIR PUBLICATION FOLLOWING THE EXHIBITION OF THE CONDITIONS AND ORDER ADOPTED IN THIS PUBLICATION: "There is in most of the great European libraries a collection of Greek manuscripts, very important for the history of the Natural Sciences, the Technology of Metals and the History of Art. The Bibliothèque Nationale de Paris contains a number of these manuscripts, and the most interesting ones. The oldest of all those known seems to date back to the end of the nineteenth century AD; it exists in Venice. He remained in Paris for two years, in the hands of M. Berthelot, as a result of a momentary loan, made with great liberality by the ItaHen Government.

“All these manuscripts have such a composition. They are formed by the same set of theoretical and practical treatises, constituting a kind of Corpus of the chemical authors, almost all of them predating the vir century of our era. The principals of these authors seem to have written in the ni' and iv" centuries, towards the times of Diocletian, Constantine, and Theodosius. The most important, Zosimus, would be contemporary with Clement of Alexandria, Porphyry, and Tertullian; he is a congenerous writer of the Gnostics and Neo-Platonists, whose ideas and imaginations he shares. The Pseudo-Democritus, on which M. Berthelot recently published an extensive article in the Journal des Sapants, which would date back to the beginning of the Christian era. Finally, the recipes relating to the dyeing of glasses and the composition of alloys are partly related, according to certain indications, to the old Egypt.

This Corpus of the Greek Alchemists was formed about the eighth or ninth century CE, in Constantinople, by Byzantine scholars, of the order of Photius and compilers of the 53 series of Constantine Porphyrogenetes, scholars who transmitted to us in analogous forms the remains of Greek science. The authors it contains are cited by the Arabs, notably in the Kitabal-Fihrist, as the source of their knowledge of chemistry. They became, through this medium, the origin of the works of Western scholars, in the Middle Ages, and consequently the initial starting point of the discoveries of modern chemistry. “Because of this connection their publication is of great importance. Moreover, they contain a multitude of processes and technical recipes, likely to throw a new light on the manufacture of ancient saws, alloys and metals: subject hitherto so obscure and so controversial in the history of the great

Vlj industries. Maspero, to whom these manuscripts have been communicated, thinks that they contain precious debris of the industrial practices and technical ideas of ancient Egypt, debris of which a complete publication alone will allow to recognize all the interest and to continue the filiation in the inscriptions of the monuments. The history of the doctrines and illusions that reigned in the world at the time of the establishment of Christianity will also draw new insights from this publication. In short, it offers equal interest, from the special point of view of the beginnings of the chemical and industrial sciences, and from the general point of view of the developments of the human mind. If this publication has not yet been made, it is because of the obscurity of the subject, the chimerical character of some of the questions treated, such as that of the transmutation of metals; finally, the difficulty of encountering the assistance of a scholar versed in the knowledge of Greek language and palaeography, with a scholar acquainted with the theories and practices of chemistry. A happy set of circumstances brings this collaboration together today. The publication in question would comprise about four to five hundred pages of unpublished Greek texts, with translation, collation of manuscripts notes and commentaries, etc. But the publication can be done in successive parts, so as to bear fruit without too great a delay and to share the expense over a certain number of years. Indeed, these texts can be classified roughly in half, in two series: historical and theoretical texts, and technical texts relating to special fabrications. Each of these two series could be divided into groups, such as the Democritan treatises, the works of Zosimas, the Commentators, the treatises on the manufacture of
Vllj

artificial glasses and precious stones; treaties on the manufacture of metals and alloys, etc. It would therefore be necessary to publish each year a half volume containing 120 to 55 pages of Greek texts, with translation, tables, etc. , which would make about 3oo to 35o pages in all each year, 1400 to i5oo pages for the whole. The publication of the figures of the apparatuses, drawn in manuscripts, and which would be reproduced by photoengraving with the perfection and absolute accuracy of modern processes, would greatly increase the interest of the publication. As we understand it, this would be a princeps edition, accompanied by a device developed from variants from the main manuscripts, as well as appropriate notes and comments. In the space of four to five years, one could complete this work, long desired by scholars and which would do honor to the nation that would execute it.

This report was adopted by the section of the Committee on Historical and Scientific Works, which had special responsibility for mathematical, physical and meteorological sciences, at its meeting on 12 November 1884. This report was read again before the Central Committee on 17 December 1884 and adopted as a committee, which instructed AL Berthelot to present the report and the proposal for publication to the Minister. Charmes, Director of the Secretariat, was pleased, with the zeal for the interests of science that distinguishes him, to seek the resources necessary for the execution, transmit the report and make final proposals to the Minister, who ordered the publication.

This publication takes place under the following conditions: Ch. - Em. Ruelle librarian at the library SainteGeneviève, took care of the Greek text. He first executed a fundamental copy, according to manuscript no. 299 of the Library of St. Mark, in Venice, manuscript of the end of the X century, the oldest and most authorized of all. For the parts not contained in this manuscript, the fundamental copy was made in general, according to manuscript no. 2827 of the Bibliothèque nationale de Paris, manuscript of the end of the fifteenth century, the most complete and the best, after that of Saint-Marc. The fundamental copy once established, it has been collated with the main manuscripts of the National Library, such as the n°' 2325 (xui century), 2275, 2326, 2329 (xvi'-xvii'' century), 2249  2447 (xvf century), 225o, 225 I and 2252 (xvii" century), 2419 (xv century), and some others: in all twelve manuscripts studied in depth. The main variants, resulting from this set of snacks, have been transcribed into note; traail made doubly considerable, by the need to identify all the variants of the manuscripts, and then to make a suitable choice between these variants. In some cases where variants are more important and extensive, they have been given in the text itself, as parallel drafting. Ruelle has attached to these variants a large number of philological notes. He also intends to publish a notice on manuscripts and a list of new words encountered in the course of his work. There would have been some advantage in pursuing these comparisons in a complete way, by studying all the manuscripts of the same collection that exist in the principal libraries of Europe, manuscripts on which M. Kopp (Beitrge lur Geschichte der Chemie, 1869, p. 254 to 340) has gathered information

very extensive and very interesting, drawn from their printed catalogues. But these manuscripts are very numerous, and disseminated. Their snack would have required many years, and the work would have become almost unexecutable by its duration and complication.
We had to limit ourselves to the twelve manuscripts above; which is already a very great work.
However, the publishers, in the desire not to omit any important work, thought it useful to have a special examination carried out, not only of the printed catalogues of the various

Libraries of Europe, but also some manuscripts that had been reported as likely to contain pre-century treatises missing from the two fundamental manuscripts taken as the basis of our work, that of St. Mark and No. 2827 of Paris. These are the manuscripts of the Vatican,
Leide and Escorial.
André Berthelot, Senior Lecturer at the École des
High-Studies, was on the spot studying the manuscripts of the
The Vatican and Leide, and he compared their composition with that of the fundamental manuscripts. He also examined the manuscripts of the German libraries, notably those of Gotha,
Munich, Weimar, Leipsick and various others. The results of his study have been published in part in the Archives of

Scientific missions (3' series, t. XIII, p. 3. 819 to 854); they will be reported in V Introduction. Except for a short fragment of the alchemical author who took the name of Justinian, they did not provide an unknown piece; but they were very useful by the study of the figures of these manuscripts, which shed new light on the successive transformations of the alchemical apparatuses in the course of the centuries.
The main manuscript of the Escorial has been examined

Special by M. Loynes, secretary of the French embassy in Madrid, mainly from the point of view of the existence suspected of treaties specific to this manuscript. But these treatises do not exist in reality, as will be said in detail in the Introduction; this manuscript being a copy, probably direct, of that of
Venice.

The manuscripts taken as the basis of our publication therefore contain all that is essential and ancient, that is to say, prior to the Vuf century of our era, in the collection: several treatises that it has seemed useful to understand there are even of more recent date, but related with the previous ones. As for the long detail of the variants of the manuscripts which we have not examined, it is a considerable work, which will have to be done later on the basis of the present publication: we have said above that we did not think it possible to undertake it, for fear of compromising our undertaking by giving it an inordinate extent. It is already three years since its beginnings and we have only managed to finish the printing of the delivery. But the second, text and translation, is entirely in the hands of the printer, and the texts of the third delivery are almost entirely copied at the present time: we are therefore able to conduct it to the end, without interruption, and this within a period which will not henceforth exceed two years.
It is useful to warn the reader that for the publication of these texts we first attached ourselves to unpublished writings; but we thought it necessary to adjourn until further notice a
new update of some already printed treatises, such as: the work of commentator Stephaniis, author of the century, previously printed by Ideler, after a copy of Dietz, xij

made on a Munich manuscript, itself derived from that of Venice (in the work entitled Physici et medici grœci minores, t. He, p. 199 to 253, 1842); and the Alchemical Poets, printed by the same publisher (t. II, p. 2. 328 to 352). Although these impressions are not valid in various respects and do not contain variations, we thought that they would be sufficient for the time being for those who are interested in this type of study. When we reach the tarnish of our work, we reserve to return to these various treaties and even to undertake a more complete edition if time permits and if the appropriations devoted to this publication are not exhausted. Our manuscripts still contain a small treatise on weights and measures, under the name of Cleopatra, a treatise which we have also considered superfluous to reproduce, because it has already been printed several times since the time of Henri Estienne; it has also been commented on and related to similar texts by the scholars who dealt with Metrology of the Ancients, notably in the classic work of Hultsch. In general, we did not think we should understand in our publication the Greek alchemical writings after the Arabs, with the exception of certain technical treatises, transcribed in the manuscripts that we print and related with older works. There are, however, a number of Greek alchemical authors more recent than this date in library manuscripts, such as: a letter on Chrysopea by Michel Psellus, Byzantine polygraph of the xi" century, put as a preface at the head of some manuscripts (see my Origins of Alchemy, p. 240); a work by Nicéphore Blemmidès, of the 12th century (translated among others in no. 2329 of the Bibliothèque nationale); several treatises and pamphlets recorded by M. André
XUJ

Berthelot in the Vatican Library (Archives of the Scientific Missions, 3rd series, t. XIII, p. 3. 819 to 854); and various other contents in the precious Greek manuscript in folio, astrological, magical and alchemical ( century) which bears the number 2419 at the Bibliothèque nationale de Paris. The most considerable alchemical work that the latter contains is a methodical treatise, inscribed under the name of Theoctonicos, and which is the same as TAlchimie Latin attributed to Albert the Great. The existence of this work in both the Greek and Latin languages, with considerable variations elsewhere raises very curious historical problems: they will be discussed in the Introduction, based on an in-depth study of the two texts. In any case, this Greek work by Theoctonicos is later than the Arabs: it is at most the end of the thirteenth century; it therefore belongs to a much more modern period than ours; the corresponding Latin text has been published on various occasions, in the Theatrum Chemicuni and at the end of the works of Albert the Great. Manuscript 2419 has also provided us with various essential information relating to the history of alchemical notations, to the planetary list of metals and their derivatives, to the relations between the parts of man and the signs of the Zodiac, to the circles of Petrosiris to predict the outcome of diseases, circles whose analogs are found in the Papyrus of Leide, in the manuscript.

2827, etc. The Greek text being thus drawn up and defined, M. Ruelle has made it a literal translation, without worrying about obscurities or seemingly incomprehensible passages. Berthelot took up this translation essay again; with the help of his technical knowledge, he sought to draw a regular meaning from it, by conforming to the Greek text, from which he was thus led to fail.

In his turn a special revision, he demands all the indulgence of the reader for this attempt of interpretation, in a matter made triply difficult: by the obscurities of the subject, of the notations and of the technical language, the explanations of the practitioners always leaving many things implied by the mystical symbolism and the vague intention of the authors, not to mention their scientific errors; finally by the material faults of the copyists, who often understood nothing at the signs. The very language of this order of treatises was very incorrect from the beginning, as shown by the alchemical papyrus of Leide, published by M. Leemans and M. Berthelot gives a complete translation with comments in the Introduction. In short, our translation of the Greek alchemists can only be regarded as a first attempt, which will certainly be perfected as a result of later studies, to which it has no other pretensions and no other merit than to provide their first foundation.

The conditions of our advertising being thus defined, let us set out the order we have adopted. It consists of three parts, namely: An Introduction, due to M. Berthelot; A Greek text, with variants and philological notes, prepared by M. Ruelle; and a Tr. duction, due to the collaboration of the two scientists, with notes and comments by M. Berthelot. First, let’s talk about the Greek text.

We have divided the many pieces which constitute it in the manuscripts into six distinct parts, namely: A First Part, under the title of General Indicationscontains the pieces of a general character, such as: the Ancient Dedication, the Lexicon, the Nomenclatures of the Philosophical Egg, the Articles on the Serpent, on the Instrument of Hermes to Foresee the Outcome of Diseases, on the Planetary List of Metals and Their Names. the oaths, the manners of the philosophers, the assembly of philosophers, the making of the asem and the cinnabar, the processes of diplosis, and finally the Labyrinth of Solomon; that is, in all twenty pieces, which we have collected in the various parts of the manuscripts, where they are disseminated.

The second part includes the Democritan Treatises, i.e. the Pseudo-Democritus, contemporary of the anonymous authors of Leide's Alchemical Papyrus, represented by two books, namely: Physica and Mystica, a book dedicated to

Leucippus; then the philosophical treatise of Synesius (end of the fourth century); finally the long and curious written of Olympiadore (beginning of the fifth century). These are the most interesting works, from a historical and philosophical point of view.
These two parts constitute the first delivery of the Greek text, the one we are giving to the public today.

The second delivery, completely prepared and delivered for printing, also contains two parts. These are: The Third Part, the longest of all, which embraces the works or rather the fragments attributed to Zosimus, fragments collected and sometimes developed by later commentators, from various epochs, some after the seventh century. The works of Zosimas, such as us
XVJ

The composition of these fragments can be seen in the works of Hermes, who already offered the character of an extensive compilation, made towards the middle of the century of our era with the writings of Democritus and those of various lost writers, such as: Cleopatra, author of treatises on distillation, whose figures have been partly preserved in manuscripts and will be reproduced in the Introduction; Mary the Jew, author of works on the apparatuses of digestion, P. A whole alchemical literature, now lost, preceded Zosimus who had summarized it. His works have in turn been used as a basis for more recent compilations, which have been confused with the primitive text. Instead of seeking to untangle immediately such a complication, it seemed preferable to give these works, as they exist in manuscripts, by limiting ourselves to gathering together the pieces sometimes dispersed, and at the risk of interspersing more recent works. We thought that it was necessary first to put the texts in the hands of the scholars, before discussing the formation. The fourth part, also included in our second delivery, contains all the ancient works which bear an author's name, whether this attribution is apocryphal or not. These are the writings of Pelage, of Ostanes, of John the Archpriest, of Agathodemon, of Coniarius, and the technological treatise inscribed under the name of Moses, which contains pieces of various dates, some contemporary of the alchemical papyrus of the time.

As for most of his texts, will be formed from the last two parts, which are: The Fifth part, essentially technological, including the book of metallic alchemy, a much more modern treatise on goldsmithing, the work of the four elements, the Salmanas technology, the coloring of glasses and emeralds, the quenching of iron and bronze, the making of glass, beer, etc. , etc. These treatises or articles, almost all anonymous, bear the character of practical works, successively reworked in the course of the centuries; alongside certain recipes going back, it seems, to old Egypt, they sometimes contain contemporary processes of the last copy of the manuscript that transmitted them to us.

The sixth part will be devoted to commentators, such as the philosopher Anonyme and the philosopher Chrétien, authors whose writings are often confused with the current writing of those of Zosime, transcribed in the third part. This is where we will give the reprint of Stephanus and that of the poets, if the resources of our publication allow it.

The Greek text is published with an independent pagination: it is due to the conscientious work of M. Ch. - Em. Ruelle, which has collated the manuscripts made available to us and reproduces the main variants, in notes developed at the bottom of the pages.

His personal work was more extensive and more complete; but he had to restrict its impression to the present limits, reserving himself to give elsewhere, if necessary, the surplus. This is what is related to the text.
A few words about the translation. The current volume contains it, printed in a separate booklet, with special pagination. At the bottom of the pages are also

notes, constituting a perpetual, technical, historical and philosophical commentary. It is necessarily divided into six parts and three deliveries, such as the corresponding Greek text. This translation is given as clearly as possible, whenever it has been thought that one succeeds in understanding the true meaning of the processes. For the rest, we kept as close as possible to the literal meaning, leaving it to the readers to penetrate further into the interpretation of these difficult texts, and if necessary to rectify, with the help of the Greek, the errors that could have been made. Text and translation are preceded by an Introduction, forming in the current delivery nearly 3oo pages, that M. Berthelot considered it useful to write for the understanding of the text: it constitutes a kind of general introduction to the metallurgy and chemistry of the ancients. It is formed by eight chapters or memoirs, separated and independent of each othernamely: 1° A study of the Greek Papyrus of Leide, with a complete X translation of the specially alchemical papyrus, and an explanation of the recipes contained therein. It is the oldest authentic text of this order known. It was written in the thirtieth century of our era; but some of the technical processes which it contains go back much higher, these kinds of processes being transmitted from age to age. Berthelot showed how the alloy recipes for goldsmithing that this text exposes were the practical starting point of the work and attempts of the alchemists. The Pseudo-Democritus and the Pseudo-Moses in particular are very directly related to it. 2° A study of the relations between metals and plates, relations originating in Babylon; they preside over all alchemical notation and play a crucial role in the history of human beliefs and superstitions.
XIX

3° A note on the sphere of Democritus and on astrologers, with two figures of the circles of Petrosiris, in photoengravings, taken from the manuscript 241g of Paris. 4° The reproduction, according to photo-engravings, of the lists of alchemical signs and notations contained in the manuscript of

St. Mark and in the manuscript 2827 of Paris. This reproduction consists of eight plates, with translation and commentary; a small alphabetical lexicon has been attached to serve as a reference point.

5° The reproduction with 35 figures of apparatus and others, contained in the manuscript of Saint-Marc, and in the manuscript 2327 of Paris; reproduction made for the most part in photoengraving and which must therefore be regarded as as close as possible to the manuscripts. An explanation of the operations carried out with the aid of these apparatuses, as well as a comparison of the drawings of the same apparatuses, made at epochs several centuries distant from each other, have been given. This comparison constitutes a true history of the manipulations of the alchemists, as well as of the changes introduced during the course of the Middle Ages.
6° Various information and notices on some manuscripts
They are alchemical and on their filiation.
There you will find the study of an old list of works, placed at the head of the manuscript.

St. Mark; a discussion of various treatises lost since; the indication of the shortcomings that this manuscript offers in its present state; its comparison with the manuscripts 2325 and 2327 of Paris; the comparative examination of the manuscripts of the Escorial, the Vatican, Leide, etc. ; some hypotheses about the origin and filiation of our current manuscripts; a special study of the Library's manuscript 241g
Nationale de Paris and the Alchemy of Theoctonicos; finally

some indications on an Arabic manuscript of Ostanes, existing at the Bibliothèque Nationale de Paris. 7 ° A note relating to some minerals and metals from the ancient Chaldea, and from the Collections of the Louvre Museum: minerals and metals that M. Berthelot submitted to his analyses. 8° Mineralogy, metallurgy and miscellaneous notices, intended to serve as comments on the chemical and mineralogical expressions used by the alchemists. This commentary was drawn up after Theophrastus, Dioscorde, Pliny and the ancient writers, and completed with the help of the Speculum ma/us of Vincent de Beauvais, the authors contained in the Bibliotheca Chemica de Manget, the Theatrum chemicum, the Library of the Alchemical Philosophers published by Cailleau, in Paris (1754), together with the articles of the Lexicon Alchemi We also took advantage of the dictionaries of the Cange Glossarium mediœ et infimœ Grœcitatis), of Henri && Thesaurus, Didot edition), and those of modern Greek.
If the space permits, a summary of the chemical processes and methods reported in this collection will be presented at the end of this collection.

General index. Perhaps it will not be superfluous to add that the comments and explanations of the current publication must be supplemented by the work of M. Berthelot, entitled The Origins of Alchemy, a work composed largely from a first reading of our manuscripts, and in which historical facts and philosophical theories are exposed with more considerable developments.
Paris, 25 October 1887.

The Chemistry of the Ancients is known to us mainly by some articles of Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Vitruvius and Pliny the Elder on medical matter, mineralogy and metallurgy; only comments that we can attach so far to the study and analysis of the jewels, instruments, colors, enamels, vitrifications and ceramic products found in the debris of ancient civilizations. Egypt in particular, so rich in objects of this kind and which a constant tradition links to the early origins of FAlchemy, that is to say, of the old theoretical and philosophical Chemistry; Egypt, I say, has so far given us no hieroglyphic document, relating to the mysterious art of the transformations of matter.

We know the ancient science of Hermes, the sacred science par excellence, only by the texts of the Greco-Egyptian alchemists; a suspect source, disturbed from the beginning and altered by the mystical imaginations of several generations of dreamers and scoliastics.
It is in Egypt, however, I repeat, that Alchemy has arisen; it is there that the dream of the transmutation of Metals first appears and it has

He was obsessed with spirits until the time of Lavoisier. The role he played in the beginnings of chemistry, the passionate interest he gave to these first researches from which our present science came, deserve the full attention of the philosopher and historian. So we must greet with joy the discovery of the authentic texts provided by the papyri of Leide. The publication of this volume was long demanded and awaited (the I with impatience by those who are interested in the history of the ancient sciences, and the contents of the current volume, already known by a summary description of Reuvens (Letters to M. Letronne, published in Leide in i83o), seemed likely to pique the curiosity of archaeologists and chemists. Indeed, one of the main papyrus that can be found there, X the ip papyrus. 199 to 259 of the present volume), is devoted to recipes of chemistry and alchemy, to the number of one hundred and one, followed by ten articles extracted from Dioscorides. It is the oldest manuscript known today, where similar subjects are discussed: for it dates back to the end of the third century AD, after Reuvens and Leemans. This, then, would be one of those old books of Alchemy of the Egyptians on gold and silver, burned by Diocletian about 290, "that they might not be enriched by this art, and derive from it the source of riches which enabled them to revolt against the Romans.

This systematic destruction is attested to us by the Byzantine chroniclers and by the acts of St. Procopius; it is in conformity with the practice of Roman law for magical books, a practice which led to the annihilation of so many scientific works during the Middle Ages.

Fortunately, the papyrus of Leideyaeté subtracts and allows us to compare to a certain extent, and on an absolutely authentic text, the knowledge of the Egyptians of the last century with those of the Greek-Egyptian alchemists, whose works have come down to us by much more modern copies. Both are closely related to the information provided by Dioscorides, by Theo(i) The first volume had appeared in 1
(2) See my work: Origins of

phrasing and by Pliny on the mineralogy and metallurgy of the ancients; which seems to indicate that many of these recipes date back to the beginnings of the Christian era. They may even be much older, as technical processes are passed down from age to age. Their comparison with the notions now acquired about Egyptian metals (i), on the one hand, and with the alchemical descriptions proper, on the other hand, confirms and specifies my previous inductions on the passage between these two orders of notions. I have endeavoured to penetrate these texts more deeply, by bringing together both the insights drawn from the history of the mystical beliefs of the ancients and their technical practices, with those provided by current chemistry: I proposed above all to seek new documents on the origin of the ideas of the alchemists relating to the transmutation of metals, ideas that seem so strange.
My today.

Hope has not been deceived; indeed, I believe I can establish that the study of these papyruses takes a step forward, by showing precisely how the alchemical hopes and doctrines on the transmutation of precious metals were born from the practices of Egyptian goldsmiths to imitate and falsify them.
The very name of one of the oldest alchemists, Phimenas or Pammenes, is found both in the papyrus and in the Pseudo-Democritus, as that of the author of nearly identical recipes.

Strange destiny of these papyrus! These are the notebooks of a forger and a charlatan magician, preserved in Thebes, probably in a tomb, or, more precisely, in a mummy. After having escaped by chance the systematic destructions of the Romans, accidents of all kinds for fifteen centuries, and, perhaps more seriously, the self-interested mutilations of the merchant fallahs of antiquity, these papyrus today furnish us with an unparalleled document for appreciating both the industrial processes of the ancients to manufacture alloys, their psychological state and their very prejudices regarding the power of man over nature. The almost absolute concordance of these texts with some of those of the Greek alchemists comes, I repeat, (1) Origins of Alchemy, p. 1 1 support by authentic proof what we could already induce on the origin of the latter and on the time of their composition. At the same time the precision of some of the recipes common to the two orders of documents, recipes still applicable today and sometimes in accordance with those of the Roret Manuals, opposed to the chimerical claim to make gold, adds a new astonishment to our mind. How can we account for the intellectual and mental state of the men who practiced these fraudulent recipes, intended to deceive others by mere appearances, and who had nevertheless ended up deluding themselves, and by believing that, with the help of some mysterious rite, the effective transformation of these alloys, like gold and silver, into real gold and silver?

In any case, we must thank Mr. Leemans to have finished on this point, with a zeal that old age has not exhausted, a work begun in its mature age, ilyaquarante-two years. It is part of the extensive publication of Leide's papyri, which he has been pursuing for nearly half a century. Moreover, the Greek papyri constitute only a relatively small part of it; they complete the earlier impressions of the Greek papyri of Paris (i), Turin and Berlin (2). I have already examined these from the cliimic point of view (3), as well as those of Leide, according to the indications of Reuvens (4) alone. It is now necessary to carry out a more in-depth study of the latter, using the complete text now published: I will make this study especially from the chemical point of view, on which I can bring the insights of a specialist, reserving the philological discussion of the texts to more competent scholars.
Let us first recall the origin of the Greek papyri of the museum
Leide; then we will summarily describe the principal writings contained in the

They are closely related to each other, by the place where they were found and even by some references from the purely alchemical Papyrus X to the specially magical Papyrus V. The history of magic and Gnosticism is closely linked to that of the origins of Talchemy: the current texts provide in this regard new evidence in support of what we already knew (i).
The last papyrus is especially chemical. I will examine the recipes in more detail, giving the translation if necessary, as far as I have been able to make it intelligible.

The Greek, demotic, and hieroglyphic papyri of Leid come mostly from a collection of Egyptian antiquities, collected at the beginning of the 19th century by the knight of Anastasis, viceconsul of Sweden in Alexandria. In 1828 he sold the collection to the Dutch government. Many of them have since been published by Dutch government orders. I'll only take care of the Greek papyrus. They form, I repeat, two volumes in-40, one of

144 pages, the other 3 10 pages: this one appeared last year. The Greek text is accompanied by a Latin version, notes and an index, and finally by plates representing the facsimile of a few lines or pages of the manuscripts. As far as the boards are concerned, we must regret that Mr. Leemans did not think it necessary to make this reproduction, at least for the second volume, by the process of photo-engraving on zinc, which provides so cheaply texts so sharp, absolutely identical with manuscripts and capable of being drawn typographically in a direct way (2). The lithographed plates of the Papyri grœci are much less perfect and give only an incomplete idea of these old writings, clearer in reality, as I have been able to ascertain on photographic proofs that I owe to the kindness of M. Revillout.

Nor will I dwell in Volume II, at Papyrus Y, which contains only an alphabet, nor at Papyrus Z, found at Philoe, very much later than the others; for it was written in Tane Sqi of our era, and contains the petition of Apion,--EvSque of the legion which held garrison at Syene, Counter-Syene, and Elephantine. Instead, let us carefully describe the three magical and alchemical papyri.

The papyrus V is bilingual, Greek and demotic; it is 3'' long, 60, 24 centimeters high; the demotic text occupies 22 columns, each one long? o 35 lines. The Greek text occupies 17 columns of unequal length. The beginning and the tin are lost. He seems to have been found in Thebes. It was written about the 111th century, according to the style and form of the writing, as from the analogy of its contents with the Gnostic doctrines of Marcus. The Greek text is poorly cared for, filled with repetitions, solecisms, case changes, misspellings attributable to the local mode of pronunciation, such as a, for and reciprocally; z: for'.. J is for C, etc. It contains magic formulas: recipes for philtras, for incantations and divinations, to provide dreams. These formulas are filled with barbaric or pleasure-forged words and analogous to those read in Jamblicus (De Mysteriis Egyptiortim) and in the Gnostics. Let us give only the following incantation, which does not lack grandeur. The gates of heaven are open; the gates of the earth are open; the road to the sea is open: The road to the rivers is open; My spirit has been heard by all gods and geniuses; My spirit has been heard by the spirit of heaven; My spirit has been heard by the spirit of the earth; My spirit has been heard by the spirit of the sea; My spirit has been heard by the spirit of the rivers.
This text recalls the refrain of a cuneiform tablet, quoted by F. LenormanJ in his work on magic among the Chaldeans.
Spirit of heaven, remember.
Spirit of the earth, remember.

In the current papyrus we find the trace of the old Egyptian doctrines, disfigured by the forgetfulness where they began to fall. Jewish names, such as Jao, Sabaoth, Adonai, Abraham, etc. , that of the Abraxa, the importance of the magic ring whose stone bears the figure of the snake biting its tail, ring that provides glory, power and wealth i), the preponderant role attributed to the number seven (2'. , "number of the letters of the name of God, according to the harmony of the seven tones", the invocation of the great name of God (3), the quotation of the four bases and the four winds: all this recalls the Gnostics and especially (41 the followers of Marcus, in the middle of the century of our era. The engraved stones of the Bibliothèque nationale de Paris also bear the figure of the snake oiiroboiOS, with the seven vowels and various cabalistic signs (5) of the same order. This snake also plays a fundamental role in Alchemy. The name of Jesus appears only once in the papyrus, in the middle of a magic formula (6) and without proper attribution. The papyrus therefore has no Christian ties. On the other hand, Egyptians, Greeks and Hebrews are frequently brought together and paralleled in invocations (Col. 8, 1. 1 5): which is characteristic. Note also the name of the Parthians ij who disappeared before the middle of the in century of our era and which is no longer mentioned later; it appears in papyrus V, as well as in one of the writings of the alchemist Zosimas. Several authors are mentioned in the papyrus, but they belong to the same kind of literature. Some, such as Zminis the Tentyrite, Hemerius, Agathocles and Urbicus, are magicians, unknown elsewhere. But ApoUo Béchès (Horus the hawk or Pebechius), Ostanès, Democritus and Moses, himself, already figure in

The same title in Pliny Faancière, and they play a great role in the alchemists. On the contrary, in the papyrus, Agathodemon is not yet ephemerized and transformed into a writer, as in the latter: it is always the divinity "in whose magical name the earth runs, hell is troubled, rivers, sea, lakes, fountains, are struck with freezing, rocks break; the one whose sky is about the head, Tether the body, and the fountains. V, col. 7, 1. 3o). Therein lies a greater index of antiquity.

Three passages deserve special attention for Fhistoirc of science; these are: the sphere of Democritus, astrologico-medical; the secret names given to plants by the sacred scribes and alchi recipes; mique. The mixing of these notions, in the same papyrus, with incantations and magical recipes, is characteristic. I will devote a special article to the sphere of Democritus and the figures of the same order that exist in several Greek manuscripts.
The sacred names of plants give rise to analogous approximations between the papyrus, the alchemical writings and the work, all scientific.

The plants and other things they used for the images of the gods were designated by them in such a way that, failing to understand them, one did vain work, following a wrong path. But we have taken interpretation from many descriptions and hidden information. 37 names of plants, minerals, etc. , the real names being placed next to the mystical names. These are drawn from blood, semen, tears, bile, feces and various organs (head, heart, bones, tail, hair, etc.) Greced Egyptian gods (Hephaistos or Vulcan, Hermes or Mercury, Vesta, Helios or Sun, Cronos or Saturn, Hercules, Ammon, Ares or Mars); animals (snake, ibis, cynocephalus, pig, crocodile, lion, bull, hawk), finally man and his various parts (head, eye, shoulder). The seed and the blood continually reappear there: serpent's blood, Hephaestus' blood, Vesta's blood,

The eye, etc. ; lion's seed, Hermes' seed, Ammon's seed; ibis's bone, doctor's bone, etc. This bizarre nomenclature is found in Dioscorides. In describing the plants and their uses in his Medical Matter, he gives the synonyms of Greek names in Latin, Egyptian, Dacian, Gaulish, etc. , synonymy that contains valuable information. It also shows the names of the works which bore the names of Ostanes (i), Zoroaster (2I, Pythagoras (3), Petesis (4), authors also cited by the alchemists and by the Geoponicians. The names given by the prophets (5), that is to say by the priestly scribes of Egypt, are specially read: I have noted 54 of these names, formed precisely according to the same rules as the sacred names of the papyrus: blood of Mars, of Hercules, of Hermes, of Titan, of man, of ibis, of cat, of crocodile; blood of the eye of Hermius; seed of Hermius; seed of Hermius.
Python; rat tail, scorpion, ichneumon; rat nail, ibis; Juno tears, etc.

There is still in the popular botanical nomenclature more than one plant name of this species: ox's eye, lion's tooth, dog's tongue, etc. , which name perhaps goes back to these old symbolic denominations 6). The word dragon blood refers today to the same drug as in the time of Pliny and Dioscorides. These names offered, from the beginning, many variants. For, in papyrus as in Dioscorides, the same name sometimes applies to two or three different plants. Thus the name of the seed of Hercules designates, in the papyrus, the rocket; in Discorides, the saffron (I, 25? , the sylvestrian myrtle iIV, 144) and the elleborus (IV, 148). Cronos blood means cedar oil and pork milk, in the papyrus. Other names have a different meaning in the papyrus and in Dioscorides, though unique in each of them. Thus the seed of Hermes means the anise in the papyrus; the bupthalmon

134; II, 144, i52, i65, 180, etc. ; III, 6, 26, 28, etc. ; IV, 4, 23, etc. (6) However, these popular names A are rather intended to make an image. As such, they could have preceded the symbolic nomenclature and suggested the idea in Dioscorides (III, 146. Bull blood means the egg of the beetle in the papvrus, the Marrubiiim in Dioscorides (III, 109). Conversely, the same plant may have two different names in both authors. Artemisia is called blood of Vulcan in the papyrus, human blood in Dioscorides (III, 1 17). Only one name is found both in the papyrus and in Dioscorides, that of Vanagallis, designated by the word: blood of the eye. We see that the nomenclatures of the botanists at that time varied no less than those of our time, even though they proceeded from common symbolic conventions, like those of the Egyptian prophets. Some of these symbolic words passed to the alchemists, but with a different meaning; these are the names: seed of Venus, taken for the flower loxide, carbonate, etc.) Of copper; of serpent's bile, taken for mercury, or for divine water; of serpent's ejaculation, taken for mercury; of Osiris (he, taken for lead (or sulphur); of black cow's milk, taken for mercury from sulphur (2); of gnat's blood, taken for alabastron's water; of Vulcan's mud (or lees), for barley, etc. ; all designations taken from the old alchemical lexicon. In the papyrus and in Dioscorides, we often find the same words, but with another sigilification. These various mystical languages reappear a little further, after an invocation to Hermes and at the head of a Gnostic narrative of creation, a narrative which I reproduce by abbreviating it, in order to give a more complete idea of this kind of literature which has had such a considerable historical role.
The God of nine forms greets you in hieratic language. and adds:

I am ahead of you, Lord. Saying so, he applauded three times. God laughs: cha, cha, cha, cha, cha, cha, cha (seven times), and God having laughed, were born the seven gods who understand the world; for they are they who first appeared.

He laughed for the second time: it was all water. When the earth heard the sound, it cried out and bowed, and the water was divided into three.
God appeared, he who is over the abyss; without him water can neither grow nor diminish.
At the third burst of laughter of God, Hermes appears; at the fifth, the

Fate, holding a balance and representing Justice. Its name means the boat of the celestial revolution: another reminiscence of the old Egyptian mythology. Then comes the quarrel of Hermes and Fate, demanding each for himself justice. At the seventh laugh, the soul is born, then the Pythian serpent, who foresees everything.

I have cited, in short, all this Gnostic travesty of the biblical account of the seven days of creation, in order to show its great resemblance to the PJstis Sophia and the congeneric texts, and to highlight the environment in which the first alchemists lived and thought.

We shall now examine Papyrus X, the most especially chemical: it testifies to a very subtle and advanced science of metal alloys and colorations, a science whose aim was the manufacture and falsification of gold and silver materials: in this respect, it opens new days on the origin of the idea of the transmutation of metals. Not only is the idea analogous; but the practices expounded in this papyrus are the same, as I shall establish, as those of the oldest alchemists, such as the Pseudo-Democritus, Zosimas, Olympodorus, Pseudo-Moses. This demonstration is of the utmost importance for the study of ori-  (i) See above (e.g. i6, note 3) the seven /,:, from the book Panaretos.

It proves, in fact, that these origins were not founded on purely chimerical imaginations, as has sometimes been believed; but they were based on positive practices and real experiences, with the aid of which imitations of gold and silver were made. Sometimes the manufacturer limited himself to deceiving the public, without being deluded about his processes; this is the case of the author of the recipes for papyrus. Sometimes, on the contrary, he added to his art the use of magic formulas or prayers, and he became duped by his own industry. The definitions of the word  gold, in the Greek alchemical lexicon which is one of the old manuscripts, are very characteristic: they are three in number, which are: call white gold, dry and yellow, and the gilded materials, with the help of which solid dyes are made; and this: "Gold is pyrite, and cadmie and sulphur;" or else: "The gold fragments are all:"

A certain analogous confusion reigns even in our day, in common language; but it does not reach the bottom of ideas, as it did formerly. Because of the very confused notions that we had then on the constitution of matter, we thought we could go further and we imagined that we could achieve it by mystical/ideal artifices. But to achieve the goal, it was necessary to implement the slow actions of nature and those of a supernatural power.

Hence the need to involve prayers and magic formulas, either to ward off enemy demons or to reconcile divinity.

Such was the scientific and moral milieu in which beliefs in the transmutation of metals developed: it was important to recall this. But it is of the highest interest, in my opinion, to see what were the actual practices, the positive manipulations of the operators. Now these practices are revealed to us by the papyrus of Leide, in the clearest form and in accordance with the recipes of the Pseudo-Democritus and Olympus. We are thus led to study in detail the recipes of the papyrus, which contains the first form of all these processes and doctrines.

In the Pseudo-Democritus, and even more in Zosimas, they are already complicated by mystical imaginations and then came the commentators, who amplified more and more the mystical part, obscuring or eliminating the practical part, to the exact knowledge of which they were often strangers. The oldest texts, as often happens, are here the clearest.

Let us first give what is known about the origin of this papyrus, as well as its X description. The papyrus was found in Thebes, probably with the two previous ones; because the recipe i5 which is found there refers to the refining process

It contains sixteen pages of writing, from twenty-eight to forty-seven lines, in capital letters of the end of the ni" century. It contains seventy-five metallurgy formulae, intended to compose alloys, for the manufacture of cuts, vases, images and other objects of goldsmithy; to weld or superficially color the metals; to try their purity, etc. ; formulas arranged without order and with many repetitions. In addition, there are fifteen formulas for making letters of gold or silver, a subject related to the previous one. The whole thing looks singularly like the workbook of a goldsmith, operating sometimes on pure metals, sometimes on alloyed or falsified metals. These texts are full of idiosyncrasies, spelling mistakes and grammar mistakes: this is the practical language of an artisan. They also offer the stamp of great sincerity, without a shadow of quackery, despite the professional Timprobity of the recipes. Then come eleven recipes to dye the fabrics in purple color, or in glaucous color. The papyrus concludes with ten articles from the Medical Matter of Dioscorides, relating to the minerals used in previous recipes. We see by this enumeration that the same operator practiced goldsmithing and dyeing of precious fabrics. But it seems foreign to the manufacture of enamels, vitrifications, artificial gemstones.

We are dealing, I repeat, with several collections of recipes of various dates and origins, put together. This is confirmed by the repetitions we encounter there. Other recipes are reproduced, once in short, another time with development: for example, the preparation of the gold solder, the writing in gold letters by means of an amalgam of this metal, the same writing by means of sulfur and the body called alum. By discussing these repetitions more closely, one could try to reconstruct the original collections, if this work seemed to have some interest.

I have carefully collated the ten articles extracted from Dioscorides, all relating to minerals used in recipes, and which give the measure of the mineralogical knowledge of the author of the papyrus. They concern the following bodies: Arsenic (our orpiment); Sandaraque (our realgar); Misy (basic iron sulphate, mixed with copper sulphate); Cadmie (impure zinc oxide, mixed with copper oxide, or even with lead oxide, antimony oxide, arsenous acid, etc.); Cadmie (other zinc oxide, mixed with copper oxide, or even with zinc oxide; The text of the papyrus on these various points is, in short, the same as the text of the known manuscripts of Dioscorides (Sprengel edition, 1829); except that the author of the papyrus has suppressed the therapeutic virtues of the minerals, the details of the preparations and often that of the provenances. These suppressions, that of medical properties in particular, are obviously systematic.
As for the detailed variants, they are numerous; but most are of interest only to grammarians or publishers of Dioscorides.

I only note that, in the article Cinnabar, the author of the papyrus distinguishes under the name of minium the cinnabar of Spain; while Sprengel adopted the variant ammion (sand ore): this confusion between the name of the cinnabar and that of the minium also exists in Pliny and elsewhere. In any case, the phrase is missing from the papyrus: either the copyist has deleted it for short; or it did not then exist in the manuscripts, having been intercalated later by some annotator.

Another variant is not without interest, from the point of view of the discussion of the texts, in the article Mercury. The text given by Sprengel reads: "Mercury is kept in glass, or lead, or tin, or silver vessels; for it gnaws away all other matter and flows. The mention of glass is accurate; but that of the vessels of lead, tin, and silver is absurd; for it is precisely these metals that mercury attacks: it could only have been added by an ignorant commentator. Now the papyrus shows that it is really so: for it speaks only of glass vessels, without mentioning metal vessels. Zosimas also insists on this point. It is known that mercury is now transported in iron vessels, the use of which does not seem to have been known to the ancients. Let's go to the really original part of the papyrus.

sections.h: EXPLANATION OF RECIPES FOR LEIDE PAPYRUS
p: These texts being known, it is now a question of bringing them closer together and of drawing certain consequences from them. The receipts for metals are the most numerous and the most interesting. They show first of all the correlation between the profession of the goldsmith, who worked precious metals, and that of the hierogrammat or sacred scribe, obliged to trace on the monuments of marble or stone, as well as on the books in papyrus or parchment, characters of gold or silver: the recipes given for gilding the jewels in the papyrus are in fact the same as for writing in letters of gold. We shall begin with this last order of recipes, the applications of which are all special, before going into the details of the metal preparations; for they form in some way the introduction to the processes of dyeing of metals. I . Recipes to write in golden letters. The art of writing in letters of gold or silver was of great concern to the artisans who used our papyrus; there are no less than fifteen or sixteen formulas on this subject, also treated several times in the manuscripts of our libraries; Montfaucon and Fabricius have already published several recipes, taken from these last. Quickly recall those of papyrus: Gold leaves crushed with gum (53) and (78). This process is still present today in Miinîie/ /îorei it. In another more complicated preparation (74), orpiment, celandine, turtle bile and saffron are combined, following a composite recipe. Orpiment appears here as a material used for its own color, and not as a dye of metals, a use he later took. We find again a recipe 1621 to write in letters of asem mlliage of silver and gold; by means of couperose, sulphur and vinegar; that is to say, without gold or silver; and a recipe 179) to write in letters of silver, with litharge released in the dove's fiente and vinegar. There are now similar recipes in the Roret II Manual, p. 140; 1 83 2): "Sprayed tin and gelatin, we form a coating, we polish with browning; we add a layer of varnish with oil or lacquer gum, which provides a white, or golden color, on wood, on leather, iron, etc. If I have given a few details about these recipes for writing letters of gold or silver, it is because they clearly characterize the people for whom they were intended. These are, I repeat, precise formulas of practitioners, of particular interest to the scribe who transcribed this papyrus, and to the whole class, so important in Egypt, hierogrammats; for it was not only a question of writing and drawing on papyrus, but also of writing and drawing on papyrus.

Manipulation of Metals

Let us come to the formulas relating to the handling of metals. They bear the trace of a common concern: that of a goldsmith preparing metals and alloys for the objects of his trade, and pursuing a double purpose. On the one hand, he sought to give them the appearance of For and silver, either by a superficial dyeing or by the manufacture of alloys containing neither gold nor silver, but capable of making illusions to unfit people and even to trained workers, as he expressly says. On the other hand, it aimed to increase the weight of gold and silver by the introduction of foreign metals, without changing its appearance. These are all operations to which the goldsmiths of our day are still engaged; but the State has imposed on them the use of special marks, intended to define the real title of the jewels tried in the official laboratories, and it has carefully separated the trade of the forgery, that is, the imitations, as well as that of the doubled, of the trade of authentic metals. Despite all these precautions, the public is continually disappointed, because they do not and cannot know the control marks and moves. There are special temptations: professional fraud does not always seem, in the minds of people in the trade, to fall under the rules of common probity. The price of gold is so high, the profits resulting from its replacement by another metal are so great, that, even today, there is incessant pressure on the part of goldsmiths in this direction, pressure which the public authorities have difficulty in resisting. Its object is either to lower the title of the gold alloys used in goldsmithing, while selling them as pure gold; or to sell at the price of the total weight, estimated as gold, the jewels containing enamels or pieces of iron or other metals; even in our time, this is a tradition common to all.

Thank you for not being able to ban. Already in the last century, at the time of the trades organized by corporations, it was said: “It seems that the art of deceiving has its principles and rules; it is a tradition that the master teaches his apprentice, that the whole body keeps as an important secret. Here, as in many other industries, there is a perpetual tendency to make substitutions and alterations of matter, very lucrative for the merchant and executed in such a way that the public does not notice it; without, however, putting itself in flagrant contradiction with the text of the laws and regulations. Beyond begins the crime, and it is not uncommon that the limit, is crossed. Now these laws and regulations, this rigorous separation between the industry of the false, the doubled, the plated, the imitations, and the industry of the real gold and the real silver, these legal marks? These precise means of analysis, which we have today, did not exist in the time of the ancients. The Papyrus of Leide is devoted to developing the processes by which the goldsmiths of the time imitated precious metals and gave the change to the public. The manufacture of lined and stuffed jewellery, however, are not included in these recipes, although Pliny ii has traces of them). The recipes here are purely chemical, that is to say that the intention of fraud is less obvious. From this, however, to the idea that it was possible to make imitation so perfect that it became identical with reality, there was only one step. This is the one that was crossed by the alchemists. Transmutation was all the more easy to conceive in the ideas of time, since pure metals, endowed with definite characters, were not then distinguished from their alloys: both of them bore different characteristics.

Instead of dyeing the surface of the metals, to give them the appearance of gold or silver, the Egyptian goldsmiths learned early to dye them thoroughly, that is to say, by modifying them in all their mass. The processes employed by them consisted in preparing gold and silver alloys retaining the appearance of metal: this is what they called the ii/p/05 /, the art of doubling the weight of silver (see above p. 56); an expression quiassed to the alchemists, at the same time as the claim to thus obtain metals, not merely mixed, but thoroughly transformed. The current word rfoiiii/e refers to the same order of ideas, but with a completely different meaning, since today it is two superimposed metal blades. In the ancients the meaning was more extensive. Indeed, the word if;j? /osî5 formerly implied, sometimes the simple increase in weight of the precious metal, added a metal of lesser value that did not change its appearance, (16) and 17, 56 . 87 and 88: sometimes the manufacture of all gold and silver coins, by the transmutation of the nature of the superadded metal; all the metals being at the bottom identical, in accordance with the Platonic theories on the
raw material. The very agent of the transformation is a portion of the anterior alloy, acting as a ferment.

All of these preparations are as clear and positive, except for the uncertainty about the meaning of a few words, as our current recipes. It is all the more surprising that, in the midst of such precise technical processes, the chimera of a true transmutation is born; it is also correlative with the intention of falsifying metals. The forger, by dint of deceiving the public, ended up believing in the reality of his work; he believed in it, as well as the dupe he had at first proposed to undo. Indeed, the relationship of these recipes with those of the alchemists can now be completely established.

III. Manufacture of Asèin.
The crux of the matter is in the making of the asem.
The asem (i) of the Egyptians originally referred to the electrum, an alloy of gold and silver, which is found in nature and which occurs easily in the

, ore processing. Its name was translated among the ancient Greeks by that which was also that of unmarked silver, that is to say, untitled, which became among the modern Greeks the very name of silver. Hence extreme confusion in the texts. But originally Yasèm.

The Egyptian language had its own meaning, as shown, no doubt, by the papyri of Leid. According to Lepsius, moreover, the asem was regarded as a distinct metal, comparable to gold and silver; it is represented next to them.

on the Egyptian monuments. It was similarly placed under the patronage of a planetary deity, Jupiter, which was later attributed to tin, around the v" or vi century of our era, when Felectrum disappeared from the list of metals. However, this alleged metal varied considerably in its properties, according to the relative doses of gold, silver, and other simple bodies, allied in its constitution; but then the thing seemed no more surprising than the variation of the properties of brass, a name which included both our red copper, and the bronzes and brasses of today. That is not all: the asem had a strange faculty: according to the treatments undergone, it could provide pure gold, or pure silver, that is to say, be changed in appearance into these two other metals. To finish characterizing these metal stains in gold and silver, as well as the entire industry of Egyptian goldsmiths and metallurgists that gave birth to Alchemy, it seems useful to give the recipes of the first alchemists themselves. I have already reproduced a few (e.g. Sg, 6i, 02, 64, 65, 67). The oldest of these recipes are set forth in the Treatise on Pseudo-Democritus, entitled Physica and Mystica; I have studied them and succeeded in drawing from them a positive meaning, about as clear as for the processes described by Pliny or Dioscorides. However, their comparison provides the most interesting results. After a technical fragment on dyeing in purple and an evocation story, this treatise continues with two chapters, one on the Chrysopia or art of making gold: the other on the manufacture of asem, assimilated to the art of making money. These two Chapters are in reality collections of recipes having the same practical character, that is to say relating as much to the preparation of superficially dyed metals, as to that of gold and silver alloys. I thought it useful to develop this study of asem, because it is new, and because it sheds much light on the ideas of the Egyptians of the first century of our era, with regard to the constitution of metals. We see that there are no less than twelve or thirteen distinct alloys, referred to under the same name of asem, alloys containing gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, zinc, arsenic. Their common characteristic was to form the transition between gold and silver, in the manufacture of silverware. Nothing was more propitious than such confusion to make fraud easier, and it had to be carefully maintained by the operators. But, by an easy return to design, it has passed from the products processed in the operations to the minds of the operators themselves. The theories of the philosophical schools on the raw material, identical in all bodies, but receiving its present form from the addition of the fundamental qualities expressed by the four elements, have encouraged and excited this confusion. Thus the workers accustomed to composing alloys simulating gold and silver, sometimes with such perfection that they themselves were mistaken, ended up believing in the possibility of actually manufacturing these metals from scratch, using certain alloy combinations, and certain turns of hand, supplemented by the help of supernatural powers, sovereign masters of all transformations.

This phrase of Jamblicus the Neoplatonic would not be disavowed by astronomers and modern physicists; for it expresses the unity of the laws of nature and the general connection of the Universe. The first perception of this unity goes back to the day when men recognized the fatal regularity of the revolutions of the stars: they immediately sought to extend the consequences to all material and even moral phenomena, by a mystical generalization, which surprises the philosopher, but which it is nevertheless important to know, if one wants to understand the historical development of the human mind. It is the golden chain that connected all beings, in the language of the authors of the Middle Ages. Thus the influence of the stars seemed to extend to all things, to the generation of metals, minerals, and living beings, as well as to the evolution of peoples and individuals. It is certain that the sun regulates, by the flux of its light and heat, the seasons of the year and the development of plant life; it is the principal source of the energies present or latent on the surface of the earth. The same role was formerly attributed, though in more limited orders, to the various stars, less powerful than the sun, but whose course is subject to such regular laws. All the historical documents prove that it was in Babylon and Chaldea that these imaginations were born; they played an important role in the development of astronomy, closely linked with astrology from which it seems to have emerged. Alchemy is also attached to it, at least by the assimilation established between metals and planets, assimilation derived from their brilliance, their color and their very number. The use of the week was ancient in Egypt and Chaldea, as evidenced by various monuments and the account of creation in Genesis. But it did not exist in classical Greece and it did not become common in Rome until the time of the Antonines. It was only in the time of Constantine and after the triumph of Christianity that it was recognized as a legal measure of civil life: since then it has become universal among the peoples of Europe. By chance, the number of wandering stars (planets), visible to the naked eye, that circulate or seem to circulate in the sky around the earth amounts to precisely seven: these are the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn. Every day of the week a star was assigned in the East: the very names of the days, as we now pronounce them, continue to translate, without our knowledge, this Babylonian consecration. Next to the seven Gods of the igneous spheres, the Chaldeans invoked the seven Gods of heaven, the seven Gods of the earth, the seven evil Gods, etc. According to François Lenprant the cuneiform inscriptions mention the seven black stones, worshipped in the main temple of Ourukh in Chaldea, bêtyles personifying the seven planets. It is to the same rapprochement that undoubtedly refers a passage from Philostrate's novel on the life of Apollonius of Tyana (III, 41), in which seven rings are mentioned, given to this philosopher by the Brahmin Larchas. The knowledge of the planetary deities of the week did not spread in the Greco-Roman world until the 1st century AD. Pompeii has a painting depicting the seven planetary deities.

All these attributions are closely related to the history of astrology and alchemy. Indeed, in the minds of the authors of the Alexandrine period these are not mere approximations; but they are the very generation of metals, supposed to be produced under the influence of the stars in the bosom of the earth.

Proclus, Neoplatonic philosopher of the 5th century CE, in his commentary on Plato's Timaeus, states that "natural gold and silver and each of the metals, like other substances, are generated in the earth under the influence of the celestial deities and their Huves. The Sun produces gold; the Moon, silver; Saturn, lead, and Mars, iron” (p. 14 C).
The definitive expression of these astrological-chemical and medical doctrines is found in the Arabic author Dimeschqî, quoted by Chwolson on the

According to this writer, the seven metals are related to the seven shining stars, by their color, their nature and their properties: they contribute to form the substance. Our author explains that among the Sabeans, heirs of the ancient Chaldeans, the seven planets were worshipped as deities; each had its temple, and, in the temple, its statue made with the metal dedicated to it. So the Sun had a golden statue; the Moon, a silver statue; Mars, an iron statue; Venus, a copper statue; Jupiter, a tin statue; Saturn, a lead statue. As for the planet Mercury, its statue was made with an assemblage of all the metals, and in the hollow a large quantity of mercury was poured. These are Arab tales, reminiscent of alchemical theories about metals and mercury, which are considered their raw material. But these tales are based on old disfigured traditions, relating to the worship of the planets, Babylon and Chaldea, and their relationship to metals.

p: The sphere of Democritus, inscribed in Papyrus V of Leide, represents the work of one of those astrologers or physicians of whom the ancients speak. They predicted the outcome of the diseases. Horapollon; I, 38) cites such calculations, and there is a treatise attributed to Hermes on this subject, in the Physici et medici groeci minores d'Ideler (i). The prediction was usually made with the help of a circle or a numerical table; it was based on a calculation, in which the age of the patient, the sum of the numerical values answering the letters of his name, the duration of his illness, etc. , combined with the day of the month and the phases of the lunar revolution. I found six such figures in the alchemical and astrological manuscripts of the National Library.

It seemed to me of some interest to bring these various paintings and circles closer to the sphere of Democritus, contained in the Papyrus V, as well as the instrument of Hermes, transcribed in the manuscript 2327. Indeed the names of Hermes and Democritus, as well as the existence of the painting of the Papyrus, establish the antiquity of these practices, contemporary of the first alchemists: they show the oriental and especially Egyptian origin. We see at the same time, by a new proof, how the name of
Democritus, in Hellenizing Egypt had become that of the head of a school of astrologers and magicians; all in accordance with the traditions which I have expounded and discussed elsewhere.

The alchemists had, like the chemists of our day, particular notations and nomenclatures: these notations were constructed, at least in part, according to precise methods and which even recall, in some respects, our present conventions. Old alchemical texts, dating back to the time of Roman regvpte and the Antonines, often result from the little intelligence we have of these notations. They are however necessary to know, for those who want to research the doctrines and practices of Chemistry, Medicine, Pharmacy, Metallurgy and Mineralogy, in antiquity and the Middle Ages. That's what made me want to reproduce them here. Only one author so far has tried to figure them: it is the scholar Du Cange, in the seventeenth century, in his Glossary of Greek in the Middle Ages. But this publication is very incomplete, very neglected and very incorrect. Moreover, it was not easy to transcribe these signs with perfect precision, at a time when procedures based on photography were not known. Moreover, the oldest and most beautiful manuscript that exists, that of St. Mark, in Venice at the end of the x or beginning of the x century, does not seem to have been known of Du Cange. Having had occasion for a few years to study in depth the manuscript texts of the Greek alchemists, for the composition of my work on "The Origins of Alchemy", I had reproduced in photoengraving the symbols of the manuscripts, taking as types those of the manuscript of Saint-Marc 'xi century) and those of manuscript No. 2327, the most complete that exists at the National Library of Paris, which was copied in 14th century. These symbols, as well as those of present-day chemistry, are placed in the head of manuscripts. They were built according to two different rules: one applicable to metals and their derivatives, the other to mineral substances and medical products, as well as to certain words of common use. The symbols of the metals are purely figurative: they are the same as those of the planets, to which the metals were respectively dedicated by the Babylonians; that is to say, stars under the influence of which the metals were supposed to be produced in the bosom of the Earth. 78). Among these symbols, those of the Sun and beyond Moon gold and silver' are already in the papyri of Leide. which date back to the middle of the century of our era .see p. 25 and 47). A few words, at the end, about the date on which the signs we have just reproduced go back. The signs of the planets already appear in the astronomical papyrus of the Louvre, which date back to the time of the Antonines as well as those of Leide, a little more recent. In the latter, they are also applied to gold (i), silver, and names of plants and minerals, as in our manuscripts. Some other signs, such as water, are hieroglyphics. The name of Osiris (PI. VI, 1. 7) was used, according to Stephanus [Origins of Alchemy, p. 32), to designate lead and sulphur (same sign for these two bodies, PI. V, 1. 11) among the Egyptians; in our board VI, this sign also recalls a special gold sign, located lower (PI. VI, 1. ig). The signs of medical matter are more modern than those of metals and planets. I have not found them, for example, in the pages reproduced by Lambecius [Comm. by Biblioth. Coes. , Liv. II, p. 2. i35 et seq.) and by Montfaucon [Greek palaeography, p. 202), after a famous manuscript by Dioscorides, written towards the end of the century for Juliana Anicia, daughter of Olybrius, one of the last emperors of the West (2).

Because of the importance of these signs, for the reading of alchemical and medical manuscripts, I thought it useful to make a small lexicon of the words contained in the preceding tables, with indication of the board and the corresponding line: the words have been preserved, for more sincerity, as they exist in the Manuscript, without correcting their faults and without returning them either to their regular form or to the nominative.

sections.h: FIGURES OF APPARATUS V. FIGURES OF APPARATUS AND OTHER OBJECTS
p: The alchemical manuscripts contain a number of ligures of apparatus and other objects, intended to make the descriptions of the text understood. These figures are of great interest. Some have varied in the course of time; probably because the experimenters who used these treatises modified the figures, according to their current practices. The whole forms, with the figures of stoves and appliances of a more recent era, as they are reproduced in the Bibliotheca Chemica of Manget, a very important set for the history of Chemistry.

I shall confine myself to studying the oldest of these devices; for it would be beyond the scope of the present publication to discuss its continuation and filiation up to modern times; it would also be necessary to seek the intermediaries among the Arabs and the Latin authors of the Middle Ages.

The symbolic figures would deserve special attention in this regard, by their correlation with certain texts of Zosimas, in his treatise on virtue, etc. I will quote, for example, very beautiful colored drawings, contained in the Latin manuscript 7147 of the Bibliothèque nationale de Paris, representing metals and various bodies, under the image of men and kings, enclosed within the phials where the fol operations take place. 80, 81 et seq.). In the Bible. Chemica de Manget, we also see figures of a mystical tradition, which goes back very high and probably to the symbolism of the old planetary deities.

But this side of the subject is less interesting to our chemical science than positive knowledge of the devices themselves. As far as these are concerned, I do not want to leave the study of the Greek alchemists today.
I have noted all the drawings which are found in the manuscript of St. Mark (century), in the manuscript 2325 of the National Library (thirteenth century).

and in the manuscript 2327 (xv century), as well as in the manuscripts 2249, 22 5o to 2 252, 2275, 2829, finally in the two Greek alchemical manuscripts of Leide and in the main Greek manuscript of the Vatican. I had photo-engravings executed by those in Paris and Venice, in order to avoid any uncertainty of interpretation. It is these figures that will be transcribed here: we will refer to them on the occasion, when printing the corresponding texts.

Figures from the manuscript of St. Mark. But these latter substances, as well as the bodies that determined the liquefaction of metals (mercury, sulfur, arsenic sulphides and others), upon reaching the bottom, experienced a new change. Indeed, the sublimable materials contained among these bodies and substances, when they reached the bottom of the apparatus, were brought to a high temperature; they vaporized then and went up towards the upper parts.

The retrograde character of this operation, which allowed the vapors to attack again the metal or substance placed on the keratokis, seems to have struck the operators: hence probably the de y.apy.iv:; (screwed echre), that is to say apparatus operating in a retrograde direction, given to some of these apparatuses. Devices 25, 26 and 27 did not exist on the original manuscript of St. Mark; they were added later, around the sixteenth century, probably, according to another manuscript comparable to the 232 5 (nineteenth century, but which no longer exists. The drawings multiplied of these devices to /. ,-.' in the various manuscripts, show that these devices have been of extended and prolonged use. They represent the first tests of water baths, sand baths, and especially ash baths, used even today in our laboratories for digestions. But these were at the origin of much more complicated apparatuses in which certain separations of substances, by fusion and sublimation, and certain slow reactions of melted or sublimated products, were operated on each other, or on other materials placed in the apparatuses. It is likely that it would be possible to find other traces of these devices

in the pharmacopoeias of the Middle Ages; perhaps they still exist somewhere in the East.
