p: Notices on the contents of the alchemical manuscripts of these libraries exist in the printed catalogues of European public libraries. K(ipp has collected and reconciled these notices in his Beitrage:ur Geschichte der Chemie (iSôg), p. 256 to 3i5; but without taking direct knowledge of the texts themselves. I have given myself in my Origins of Alchemy, p. 335 to 385, a more detailed analysis of the manuscript 2327 of the Paris Library and the old manuscript of the library of St. Mark, in Venice. I had compared them with each other, and with the manuscripts 2325, 2275 and 2249, which I also had in my hands, as well as with the manuscripts of the Laurentian at Florence and some others; the latter, according to the printed catalogues. The present publication will render these analyses useless for the first five manuscripts; but I thought it useful to further clarify the knowledge of certain others, such as the Vatican manuscripts, which I had examined on the spot by my son, M. André Berthelot; the two manuscripts of Leide, that of Gotha, and various manuscripts of the German libraries, examined also by my son; those of the Escurial, that M. de Loynes, secretary of embassy in Madrid, has kindly collated for some important passages; the manuscript 24 9 of the Bibliothèque nationale de Paris, 1 which I have studied myself; finally an Arabic manuscript of Ostanes, belonging to the same Library and of which I was to translate a few pages. It is this information that I am going to share. I will precede them with some precise data, drawn from the manuscripts themselves and especially from the manuscript of St. Mark, which provide new indications on the mode followed in their composition, on the relative order and filiation of their copies, and on the accidents which occurred during their successive transcriptions. The whole forms a dozen small notices on the alchemical manuscripts.
I. Old list of St. Mark's manuscript.

This list represents an older writing than the manuscript of St. Mark that it precedes, at least as we have it. It differs in composition and relative order.

From the point of view of composition, the first ten numbers are common to the list and manuscript; but the four treatises (1,(12), (13), (4 attributed to Heraclius, and the two treatises (15), (16), attributed to Justinian, have disappeared. Let us recall here that the Emperor Heraclius was a great exponent of astrology and occult sciences. His name is found in Arabic works and in the Tiirba philosophorum (in the erroneous form of Hercules).
Stephanus, his contemporary, dedicated one of his authentic lessons to him.

The treatises attributed to the Emperor Justinian are obviously pseudonymous and, according to some fragments, not very remote: perhaps it is Justinian II, one of the successors of Heraclius, at the end of the seventh century. There is still a reference to these treatises (Justinian practice) in the article of a more modern writing, added to a cover of the manuscript of St. Mark (Origins of Alchemy, p. 348. VIII. General assumptions about the origin and filiation of Greek alchemical manuscripts.

From all the observations that I have gathered, the origin of the Greek alchemical manuscripts could be established with some probability in the following way: 1° There existed in Egypt, before the Christian era, groups of technical recipes, relating to goldsmithing, to the manufacture of alloys and metals for weapons and tools, to the manufacture of glass and enamels, to the dyeing of medical materials. The use of these recipes was accompanied by certain magic formulas. The whole was traditionally transmitted, as a trade secret, since a very remote time, with the assistance of hieroglyphic signs, intended to serve as mementos, rather than to expose the details of the operations (i). These signs were inscribed on steles; they were anonymous, like all Egyptian science at the time. It seems that there were also written demotic texts on papyrus; such were

The Democritus School of Egypt has created a scientific tradition, especially in alchemy; a tradition that has continued until the seventh century AD, through a whole series of original writings and commentaries, which form the main part of our current collections. The authors who continued it at the beginning were Gnostics, pagans and Jews, who developed more and more mvstic symbolism. sections.h: VII. ON SOME METALS AND MINERALS FROM THE ANCIENT GHALDEE
p: As I continued my studies on the origins of Alchemy and on ancient metals, I had occasion to examine various materials, some from the palace of Sargon, in Khorsabad, others from the excavations of Tello by M. by Sarzec. It is thanks to the extreme obligingness of our colleague, Mr. Heuzey, curator at the Louvre Museum, that I was able to study these samples, taken from the precious collections of our great National Museum. I will present the results of my analyses, and I will then present various new or little known documents, relating to the origin of the tin used by the ancients in the manufacture of bronze. Let’s start with the items from Khorsabad. In the course of his excavations, in 1854, M. Place discovered, under one of the cornerstones of the palace of Sargon, a stone chest containing votive tablets, covered with very sharp cuneiform inscriptions, intended to recall the foundation of the building (70 BC. -C.l. According to M. In place, these tablets would have been five in number; but the inscriptions formally indicate that there were seven, designated by name. Only four of these tablets are now in the Louvre Museum. The other three are lost. The remaining four tablets have long and detailed inscriptions. Oppert published the translation of three of them, in the work entitled Nineveh and Assyria, by V. Place (t. II, p. 2. 3o3; 1870). The meaning is about the same for all three and it relates to the construction of the palace. According to this translation, the tablets were in gold, silver, copper, in two other bodies whose names have been identified with lead and tin, the latter more doubtful, according to M. Oppert: finally in two last bodies bearing the determinative of the stones used as building materials, and which are regarded as marble and Talabaster. Unfortunately, each tablet does not contain other than the name of the material it is made of. I looked at the four tablets currently in existence at the Louvre. They are rectangular and several millimeters thick. The golden blade is the smallest; it is easily recognizable, although it has lost its luster. It weighs about 167 gr. It was shaped with a hammer. The metal is not allied with another in notable proportion. The silver blade is also pure, or about. It is slightly blackened on the surface, due to the formation of a sulphide, as happens to silver exposed for a long time to atmospheric agents. It weighs about 4355 I give these weights as information, without prejudging whether they met the relative values of metals at the time the palace was founded. It is known that the value ratio of gold to silver has varied greatly according to time and place. The famous copper blade is deeply altered and partly exfoliated by oxidation. It weighs, in its present state, about 9528''. This, together with the density of the metal, less than that of gold and silver, suffices to show that the dimensions of it are much larger than those of the other two. The color is dark red, mainly determined by the presence of copper oxide. However, it is not pure copper, but bronze. Indeed, a sample taken with lime on the edges contained, according to the analysis: Tin Copper Oxygen, etc.

There is no lead, zinc or other metal in significant quantities. The proportion of tin corresponds to that of a gold-yellow bronze; but the presence of copper protoxide altered the color. This composition is also found in a large number of antique bronzes. I will mention only an Egyptian mirror, dating from the 17th or 16th century ravishes our era, and that
I used to analyze for M. Mariette. It contained 9 parts of tin and 91 of copper.

The fourth tablet is the most interesting of all, because of its composition. It weighs about I85s It consists of a bright white material, opaque, compact, hard, carefully cut and polished. It has so far been thought to be formed by a metal oxide and even originally referred to as an antimony tablet, others say tin; based on the opinion that it was once made with a metal that time would have gradually oxidized. However, neither antimony nor tin possess the urge to alter themselves in this way, especially when contained in a stone chest. At most, lead or zinc are likely to change into oxide, or carbonate, in a humid environment  but then they disintegrate and fall into dust, while the tablet is perfectly compact and covered with a very fine inscription and extreme sharpness. Its real nature was therefore a real enigma.

To examine it more closely, we first carefully conducted a survey, and found that there was no central sheet of metal in the thickness of the tablet. The chemical analysis then indicated that the tablet material is pure, crystallized magnesia carbonate, which is much more resistant to extended acids and atmospheric agents than lime carbonate. The polish of this tablet seems to have been supplemented with an almost insensitive trace of fat, which is manifested by calcination.
Let us observe here that our magnesia and its salts were unknown in antiquity and the Middle Ages, the name of magnesia having formerly had very different meanings, multiple besides i).

In Pliny, this word designates various black, white, or red minerals, coming from the cities and provinces of the same name: in particular the magnet stone or magnetic stone (which has retained the name); a mineral that seems to be our manganese oxide (other transformation of the same name); finally the iron, copper, pyrites, perhaps of tin and lead. By extension, the name magnesia was then applied to
(See this volume, p. 28. 66, i53 and beyond.
successive products: oxides and even alloys, resulting from the roasting and processing of these various pyrites.

The meaning of the word has changed even more among the Alchemists, who have tended to certain alloys and amalgams, sometimes silvery. It's only around the xv! ii century it was given to mixtures of sulphate and lime carbonate, often containing salts of magnesia; and finally to the precipitated carbonate of the salt of Epsom: the last attribution which led the word magnesia to its present meaning.

In any case, pure and crystallized magnesia carbonate is a very rare mineral, which Haiiy did not know at the beginning of this century. Its intimate association with lime carbonate generates dolomite, a rock on the contrary very widespread. Magnesia carbonate itself is mainly found in veins interspersed in talcum schist, serpentine and other magnesian silicates; it results from the slow decomposition of these schist by natural agents. The material of the tablet of the palace of Sargon contains indeed some traces of silica, which betray the same origin.

The choice of such an exceptional mineral, to make a sacred tablet, did not have to be made at random: it probably corresponded to some particular religious idea. In any case, he proves that the Assyrians knew the carbonate of magnesia as a substance of its own. To what word did this tablet really answer in Tinscription, where it appears to appear under one of the names hitherto reputed to be metallic? Despite the lack of a special name on this tablet, M. Oppert has kindly told me that it was designated by the word a-bar, previously taken for that of tin.

It seemed useful to me, in order to try to obtain some new light in this respect, to analyze the very material with which the great bulls of the Louvre Museum are built and to investigate above all whether it contained dolomite. But I have verified that it is crystallized lime carbonate, presenting the physical constitution either of marble, or rather of this variety of limestone, formerly confused under the name of alabaster with anhydrous lime sulfate. It is not for me to further discuss the philological question of the true denomination of these matters (v. This volume, p. 80). While I was studying the tablets of Khorsabad, Mr. Heuzeyappell

attention to certain metallic objects, coming from the excavations made in Tello by M. of Sarzec: it was a fragment of a vase and a votive figurine. The fragment represents a portion of a cylindrical circular cord, (jg -mm to S"""" in diameter, which formed the orifice of a molded vase, prepared by melting and pouring. We can still see a part of the throat that separated this cord from the body of the vase itself. The shape is very simple and without any delicate lines or inscription. The surface is covered with a very light patina, a yellowish black. The mass is formed by a shiny metal, black, whose break presents voluminous and shimmering crystals. The material itself is very hard, but fragile. According to the analysis, it consists of metallic antimony, substantially pure and containing at a notable dose neither copper, lead, bismuth nor zinc, but only a few traces of iron. The patina appears to be a xysulfide, formed by the action of traces of hydrogen sulphide that exist in the atmosphere. The existence of a broken fragment of vase cast in pure antimony is something singular; for the present industry does not use this pure metal for such a use, though it frequently uses its alloys, and I have seen no other analogous example in the utensils, either of the present or of the past times. However, I had been told that the Japanese use it in their fabrications and Ton even gave me a small winged dolphin, reputedly constituted by antimony. But the exact analysis of this dolphin showed that it contained zinc and various associated metals (tin, bismuth, iron), but that it was far from being formed by pure antimony. If pure antimony was really used by the Japanese, which I doubt, there would be a singular rapprochement with the ancient Chaldean industries. It is also an extremely curious circumstance that the authentic discovery of such a fragment worked of antimony, made at Tello, a place which has remained uninhabited since the time of the Parthians, and which contains the remains of the oldest Chaldean civilization. The antimony, in fact, is reputed not to have been known to the ancients and to have been discovered only around the fifteenth century. However, it must be observed that the ancients knew perfectly our antimony sulfide, a natural mineral to which they gave the name of stibium or slimmi and which they used for many uses, especially in Medicine. There is even in Dioscorides a passage reproduced by Pliny which I think can be concluded that metallic Tantimony had already been obtained at that time. We read in fact in Dioscorides [Medical matter, liv. V, ch. xcix): "This mineral is burned by placing it on coals blowing up to incandescent; your pro(-'). » runs along the fence, it changes to lead
Pliny said the same.
[Natu story! - she, ïiv. XXXIII,chap. xxxiv): "It is necessary above all to grate with

"precaution, so as not to change it to lead ne plumbum fiât)". These observations respond to phenomena well known to chemists. Indeed, the mesh of antimony sulfide, especially in the presence of coal, can easily return it to the state of fusible and metallic antimony, a substance that Pliny and his contemporaries confused, as well as all black metals and easily fusible, with lead. The existence of the Tello vase proves that there was also in Mesopotamia, and from a time probably much older, tried to prepare molded vases with this alleged variety of lead, less alterable than ordinary lead.
Since the first publication of these analyses, I have received a letter from

Virchow, who announces to me that he has printed in the Bulletiii of the Anthropological Society of Berliti (he, a Note on small ornaments in antimony, found in an ancient Transcaucasian necropolis iRedkinLager), probably dating from the time of the first introduction of iron.
This is another example of the ancient knowledge of antimony.

The votive metal figure of Tello gives rise to no less interesting observations. It represents a divine character, kneeling, holding a kind of metal tip or cone. It bears the engraved name of Goudeah, that is to say, it corresponds to the earliest epoch to which belong the objects found so far in Mesopotamia. Oppert would attribute to it an antiquity of four thousand years before our era. We thus find ourselves referred to the most remote times of histoi metallurgy. I laughed (i). This figurine is covered with a thick green patina. Below the patina is a red layer, formed by the metal, deeply altered and oxidized in most of its thickness. Then comes a red metallic core, which offers the appearance and tenacity of copper itself: it is the last remnant of the primitive metal, gradually destroyed by natural actions.
I analyzed these different parts.

Superficial green patina is a mixture of copper carbonate and hydrated copper oxychloride. The latter compound is well known to mineralogists as Aitakamite. It results from the alteration of the metal by the brackish waters, with which the figurine was in contact during the course of time.

The middle layer is approximately pure copper protoxide, containing no tin, antimony, lead or analogous metal, or zinc, at a notable dose; it is the result of a slow alteration of the metallic copper.
Finally, the core consists of metallic copper, which is very substantially pure.

The absence of any metal other than copper in this figurine is worth noting; for such objects are usually made of bronze, an alloy of tin and copper, harder and easier to work with than its components. The very absence of tin in Tello copper could offer a very special historical significance. Indeed, tin is much less widespread than copper on the surface of the earth and its transport has always been, in antiquity as today, the object of a special trade. In Asia in particular, until recently, no other deposits of tin had been reported that were somewhat abundant than those of the Sunda Islands and the southern provinces of China. The transport of this tin to western Asia was formerly by sea, to the Persian Gulf and to the Red Sea, by means of a long and painful navigation; and it was transmitted from there to the coasts of the Mediterranean, where it came to compete with the tin of the English islands.

The Phoenicians, who once came from the shores of the Persian Gulf to those of the Mediterranean, seem to have been the first promoters of this navigation, at least in the West (Strabon, liv. 111, chap. V, 1 1). In fact, I have recently learned of two documents, which are of such a nature as to fix a less distant origin on the bronze tin of Assyria and Egypt. H, 10) of the tin mines in the Drangiane, a region which answers to the south of Khorasan, below Herat, towards

But geologists have never found them in this region so far. See on this question: Anthropological research in the Caucasus, by E. Chantre, t. I, p. 1. 81 (i885), Age of Fog, t. II, p. 2. 3o5. The Western Limits of Afghanistan. But the transport of Pétain from this point to Chaldea would still have required a journey by land, of long duration, through regions where the moderns themselves come very difficult. In truth, the usual metals and their alloys seem to have been transported once throughout the world by nomadic casters, analogous to the Gypsies and who passed everywhere. The main difficulty that Ton can object to these small lodgings and to these individual transports of ctain, is the abundance and the universal diffusion of the bronze weapons, for long centuries. Previous assumptions do not seem to meet the need for such a prolonged, general and also considerable manufacturing. To satisfy it, there had to be regular transports of masses of tin, "by means of abundant and inexhaustible mines. If tin is rare in the world, it is not the same with copper. Copper ores are found on a large number of points. The mines of Sinaî, to name but a few, are famous in ancient Egypt. The extraction of metallic copper with the help of its ores is also easy. Because of these circumstances, several archaeologists have assumed that an age of pure copper, that is, an age when weapons and utensils were made with this metal, must have preceded the Bronze Age. Bronze, harder and more resistant, would then have replaced copper, as soon as it was discovered. To judge of this hypothesis and to establish the date at which these distant transports and this old navigation began, it would be necessary to possess the analysis of the oldest objects which have a certain date, among the remains of antiquity which have come down to us. But tin-based bronze already existed in Egypt, nearly two thousand years before our era, according to analyses of this kind (v. 220). The analysis of the figure of Tello seems to indicate, on the contrary, that the tin was not yet known, at the remote time of the manufacture of this object, the tin then not reaching the Persian Gulf. This is, moreover, only an induction, some religious or other circumstance which may have determined the exclusive use of copper in this figurine: it would be necessary to examine more numerous and more varied objects for the purpose of determining the use of copper in this figurine.
It will take that to a certainty. But it seemed interesting to me to point out the general problems raised by the analysis of Tello metals.

This word was used to represent both pure copper and the very diverse alloys it forms by its association with tin, zinc, lead, nickel, arsenic, and various other metals; that is, the bronzes and brasses of the moderns. The word copper, even nowadays, is sometimes used in such a comprehensive sense: red copper, yellow copper, white copper, etc. ; while the word brass, in the language of our goldsmiths, ended up denoting a particular alloy, formed of 9 parts of copper and 3 of zinc. But the ancient meaning of the word brass was synonymous with that of copper.
The very name of copper comes from an epithet applied to the brass of

Cyprus our pure copper was not designated by a single word among the ancient peoples, no more among the Orientals, than among the Greeks, or among the Romans; at least until the in' century of our era, when appears the word cupritm. Let us emphasize that neither the Greeks nor the ancient Romans used two distinct and specific words for copper and bronze, and that one should not look for two such names among the old Orientals.

The word oes, brass, applied indifferently to copper and its alloys with tin, lead, zinc. In order to understand the ancient texts well, it is necessary to remove from our minds the precise definitions acquired by the chemistry of our time; for simple bodies have, at first sight, no specific character which distinguishes them from their compounds. No one in antiquity looked at red copper as an element that had to be isolated, before associating it with others. The ancients, I repeat, did not conceive these alloys as we do, bringing them back to the association of two or three elemental metals, such as our copper, our tin, our lead, elemental metals that we melt together to obtain bronzes and brasses. But they worked above all on the ores of these metals, more or less pure, ores called cadmies, or chalcites; they mixed them, before making and melting the metal proper; sometimes, though they were not, they did not.
- more rarely, they joined together the alloys and metals obtained from the first jet.
All metal and alloy red or yellow, alterable to fire, was called oes; all metal and alloy white, fuse and alterable to fire, was called oes.
one lead. Later two varieties were distinguished: black lead, which included our lead and, more rarely, our antimony, etc. ; and white lead, which included our tin and some lead and silver alloys.
As for the -/'/. or where the varieties were distinguished according to the place of origin ( i

: copper of Delos, of Aegina, of Cyprus, of Syracuse, of Cordoba; or after the name of the owner of the mine: copper Sallustien, Marien, Livien i2'; without attaching to one of these varieties, the character of a metal simpler, more elementary than the others. - The only precise distinctions that we read in the ancient authors are those of the orichalk, and the brass of Corinth. The orichalque, a word whose etymology is unknown, is regarded by Hesiod and Plato as a precious metal. According to Pliny, his discovery brought the copper of Cyprus into disrepute; but the ore which supplied it was exhausted. The copper Marien approached, and was used preferably for the most expensive currencies, such as sesterces and double aces: the copper of Cyprus being reserved for the more vile currencies, such as the aces. It is known elsewhere that the value of the orichalque was at one time double that of ordinary copper: it was probably some bronze more beautiful and more resistant.

Lead: distinguished 2 species, black and white, the latter assimilated to our tin (2). Black lead was also extracted from the money. It was welded by the interlude of tin. The metal of the first casting, obtained with silver lead, was called stanmim; the second, silver; what remained in the furnace, galena. The remelted galena produced black lead. We can see that the word tamnim here means an alloy of silver and lead. As for the word galena, it did not have the same meaning as today, where it means lead sulfide.
Among the ancients, lead was often confused with its tin alloys, as well as antimony (v. 224I and bismuth, rarer metal and whose discovery is modern.

sections.h: PART I GENERAL INDICATIONS I. 1. DEDICATION
p: Look at this volume as containing a secret happiness, whoever you are who are the friend of the Muses. But if you wish to explore the veins laden with gold, which are skillfully hidden; open the keen eye of the spirit and raise it to the divine natures, with perfect insight; thus journey very learnedly written, and find in it the treasure of a superior knowledge, seeking and exploring nature three times happy, the only one that dominates natures in a divine way, the only one that inspires them. Whoever invented it, I won't say who he is. Admire intelligence, the wisdom of these divine men, creators of bodies and spirits; (Admire, I say) how they have reached the sublime height of gnosis, so as to animate, kill and vivify, to create strange figures and farms. Wonderful! Oh very happy and sovereign matter! The one who knows it thoroughly and who knows the results hidden under its riddles, this one, yes, is the intelligence worthy of all honor, it is the eminent spirit of Theodore, who enriches himself in a divine way, he the faithful defender of the prin(i)
,, do-Democritus. (2) The word "body" may be applied to, or separate from, metals (v. Introduction, p. 3. 247).

in the language of the alchemists, to me(3) These mystical expressions signi -, regenerated rates of their oxides and other minerals. The word spirit makes the production of metals, their disappearance by oxidation, dissolution, etc. , a vaguer meaning; it means specia and their regeneration.
these. He gathered, he brought a strange collection into this volume of scholarly designs. In protecting him, Christ, sovereign master, keep him in your custody.

On the Theodore to whom this Dedication is addressed. The indication of this name, which refers to a high official of the Byzantine Empire, is the only one we had on the formation of the alchemical collection. It concerns an epoch between Heraclius and the beginning of the twelfth century, date of the ms. of Venice; a period which includes those of the compilations of Photius and Constantine Porphyrogenetus (see Origins of Alchemy, p. g8). "The name Theodore is too widespread for one to hope to identify, without any other clue, the present personage with some Byzantine, known otherwise in history. In the works of Zosimus, there is also, under the title of "Chapters to Theodore", a summary of the summaries of various treatises Origins of Alchemy, p. 184). Stephanus writes similarly to a Theodore (Ideler, t. He, p. 208), which could be our character: he would then be contemporary of Heraclius.

The Alchemical Lexicon, as we have just reproduced it, is taken from the manuscript of St. Mark (end of the s." or beginning of the twelfth century): it has hardly been modified in later manuscripts. It is formed of various portions, added successively, as evidenced for example by the articles relating to sulphur, sulphur water, magnesia, etc. Some articles go back to the old Greco-Egyptian tradition, as shown by the connections (quoted in note) with the prophetic nomenclature of Dioscorides and Papyrus of Leid. The white and yellow catalogues, attributed to Democritus (0;;5 ie i'4/c/n"w/e, p. 55-i56), which formed the basis of the Chrysopia and Argyropia, as well as the nomenclatures of the philosophical egg, seem to represent the first forms of this Lexicon. In the middle ages, it took a considerable extension and was enriched with a multitude of Arabic words, at the same time that the Greek words disappeared in part. A new form of it can be seen in the manuscript 24 iq of Paris, transcribed around 1460 (v. /"iroi. , p. 3. 2o5). Several of these Lexiques were collected by Johnson in the Bibliotheca Chemica de Manget (Geneva, 1702), t. I, p. 1. 217 to 291. But the most useful work of this kind to know and best written, is the Lexicon Alchemio, auctore Rulando (Frankfurt, )2. I mentioned this frequently in my introduction.

sections.h: I. XV. ON THE ASSEMBLY OF PHILOSOPHERS
p: The philosophers sent one to another in order to form a meeting, since a quarrel and a great disturbance had assailed them; this disturbance came from the error which has befallen the world in regard to natures, bodies, and spirits, i3, touching the question of whether it is by means of several species, or only one, that the mystery is accomplished. The philosopher, clearly answering the things known to them, expresses himself thus: “It is not for those of our race, coming from a single species, to reproach us with our books and to throw imprecations at our heads. With regard to the dyeing of gold that one wants to obtain, this is what has been indicated to me by the people of the trade: If anyone comes to explain the teachings relating to the multiplicity of species, he is in error; for the goal pursued is different. The stove is unique, unique the path to follow, unique also the work.” Nothing will lead to the goal (even at the price of 5o denarii) (6). sections.h: THE LABYRINTH OF SOLOMON 1. XX. THE LABYRINTH THAT SOLOMON HAD BUILT (1)
p: Have you heard of a labyrinth which Solomon planned in his mind, and which he had built with stones gathered in circles? This drawing represents its layout, form and complication, drawn by fine lines, in a rational way. Seeing its thousand circuits, from inside to outside, its spherical roads that return in circles, here and there, on themselves, learn the circular course of life, thus showing you the slippery bends of its abruptly folded paths.
By its spherical, circular evolutions, it subtly wraps itself in compound cords; just as the pernicious snake, in its folds, crawls and slips, in a way sometimes manifest, and sometimes secret.

It has an obliquely placed door and difficult access. The more you run from the outside, wanting to launch yourself, the more he, by his sudden detours, 't'j engages inside, towards the depth where the exit is. He seduces you every day in your errands; he plays and mocks you with the returns of hope; like a dream that deceives you with vain visions, until the time that settles the comedy has passed, and the death, alas!
setting everything in the shade, received you, without allowing you to succeed in reaching the exit.
(i) See Figure 3o, Introd. , p. 3. ibj. This labyrinth is a cabalistic work of the Middle Ages, which does not belong to the old tradition of the Alchemists 2recs.

As I repeatedly invoked him, asking him how I could reconcile natures, he told me that it was difficult for him to speak without the permission of the Demon (genius). And he said only these words: “The books are in the Temple. Returning to the Temple, I began to seek if I could be put in possession of the books; for he had not told me of these books during his lifetime, having died without having made any testamentary dispositions. He had, it is claimed, taken a poison to separate his soul from his body, or else, as his son says, he had swallowed poison inadvertently. Before his death, he intended to show the books to his son only, when he had passed the first age. None of us knew anything about these books. As after having made investigations we had found nothing, we gave ourselves a terrible evil (to know) how substances and natures unite and merge. But when we had made the compositions of the matter, the time having come for a ceremony in the Temple, we made a common feast. So, as we were in the naos, all of a sudden, a certain column opened, but we saw nothing inside. But neither he nor anyone else had told us that his father’s books had been deposited there.

As we advanced, we were led to the column; as we bent down, we saw with surprise that nothing had escaped us, except this precious formula which we found there: nature enjoys nature; nature triumphs over nature; nature masters nature.
We were very surprised that he had gathered in so few words his entire writing.

In diseases that require the use of caustics, the multiplicity of remedies is useless; while lime alone, properly implemented, cures the disease. Often the variety of treatments in ophthalmia has the effect of harming; while thorny nerve is a successful plant, in any affection of this kind. We must therefore disdain this collection of vain and untimely materials and use only natural (convenient) substances. Now judge from this whether anyone can accomplish the work, without the natures previously exposed. But if nothing can be done without them, why do we love this fantasy of various materials? Why, in our country, does this concurrence of many species tending to the same result, since one nature alone triumphs over the whole? Let us see the composition of the species, in view of Argyropea.

Democritus to Leucippus, his friend, greeting (5). Know what was on these arts of the Egyptians, O Leucippus, in the books of the Persian prophets. I have written in the vulgar dialect; because it is the one that best suits the subject; but the book itself is not vulgar; for it contains mystical, ancient, and very reasonable riddles; riddles which the ancestors and kings of divine Egypt have exposed.

(i) Lime water, or milk of lime. (2) Dyeing by amalgamation. (3) In other words, the author refers to his other works on distillation. (4) This is the conclusion of the two treatises relating to the dyeing of gold and enasem, or silver; dyeing carried out sometimes on the surface, by direct coloration of the metal or varnishing; sometimes on the bottom, by manufacture of an alloy. These treatises consist of a series of recipes, congeners of those of the Papyrus of Leiden; but at the end of which the author added the mystical axioms relating to nature. The idea of true transmutation is not obvious. (5) This sentence was omitted by accident in the printed Greek text. (6) Cp. Orig. of the Alch. , p. 3. 47. As for me who am your friend, I will use reasonable riddles, such as no one wrote for me among the Egyptian initiates. You, doctor, who have an awakened mind, I will take care to explain it openly all things. The work includes bleaching and yellowing, as well as softening and baking of copper ore. I leave the tincture aside; but later I shall return to all the singular products which are made by means of the same copper and cinnabar. You can make gold with cadmie and other species, by calcinations and alloys, and make singular products. Now, the book begins like this: Take thin arsenic, and make metal sheets. Put in a round pot, and burn. Then, when (the preparation) is ready, throw in some old milk, pouring it without tilting the vase. When coagulated, remove and release with alum watered with heifer urine, for seven days then; dry in the sun; release again brine; throw in saline efflorescence (i) gar; dez for seven days, and the product forms. Take it; dry it again in the sun; put this (preparation) in a pot, cook it with castor oil or horseradish, until it turns yellow. Throw copper into it and it will whiten. The same effect is produced by sandaraque. By treating the same by green matter, half of the copper will be used for yellowing, and the other part for certain arrangements (2). This is how the treatment of sulphurous materials for copper bleaching is carried out. Taking arsenic, macerate, either in salt for nine days, or in the urine of an impuberter; or, for it is better, for twenty-one days. Then pour in vinegar 3; lemon, for seven days, mixing the white part of the lemons; then dry. Then, taking iron-colored sandarachus, put it in pieces and macerate in the brine, for twenty-one days.
Then, taking Skin and Limestone, make a liqueur, dry and preserve. Then, taking the sandaraque, boil it with oil for a while.

sections.h: H. M. SYNESIUS THE PHILOSOPHER HAS DIOSCORUS ON THE BOOK OF DEMOCRITUS.
p: To Diosconis, priest of the great Serapis, in Alexandria, with God's approval, the philosopher Synesiiis, greeting. The letter you addressed to me on the book of the divine Democritus did not leave me indifferent; far from it. With great zeal and great effort, I

(i) Or seaweed. (2) This recipe is that of a projection powder; it is too obscure for the meaning to be specified. The very name of the "golden coral" represents a preparation of which we do not know the exact meaning. (3) Synonym of lead and copper alloy. (Introd. , p. 3. i53.)

I put my mind to torture and I was looking forward to coming to you. We propose to say who was this man, the Democritus philosopher, this naturalist who came from Abdera, who directed his investigations on all things of nature and who treated of natural beings. Abdère is a town in Thrace. Democritus was a very learned man who, having come to Egypt, was initiated into the mysteries by the great Ostanes, in the sanctuary of Memphis, by him and his disciples, priests of Egypt. He composed four books of dyeing, on gold and silver, on stones and on purple. By these words, "drawing his principles," I mean that he wrote after the great Ostanes. For this writer is the first to utter these axioms: “nature is charmed by nature”; and “nature dominates nature”; and “nature triumphs over nature,” etc. But it is necessary that we seek (the meaning of the writings) of the Philosopher and learn what is the thought and what is the order of his successive teachings. That he formed two catalogues is a certain fact for us; for he made two catalogues, namely, that of yellow and that of white. First he catalogued solids, then liquors, that is, aqueous materials, although none of these are used in Art. Indeed, he himself, speaking of the great Ostanes, attests that he had not used the projections of the Egyptians, nor their cooking processes; but that he operated on the substances with plasters placed outside, and making fire act he carried out the preparation. And he said, It is the custom of the Persians to do so. But what he says means that: if

(i) The first two of these books, or their extracts, are none other than the two collections of recipes on the art of making gold (or dyeing gold) and on the manufacture of Tasem (or silver), which constitute the essential part of the Treaty entitled: "Natura-relellesetmysterious Questions". The third is lost: however, the work on the art of making glass and artificial gemstones, which we find in the Alchemical Collections, must have its first origin. As for the work on purple, there is only one remains in the head of the "Questions
“Natural.”
These various subjects have remained the common matter of the old alchemical treatises, as evidenced by the title I have reproduced (Origins of Alchemy, p. i23) and the content of the
Moses' treatise, given further on.
(2) The Philosopher par excellence, Democritus.
(3) This passage seems to distinguish between coloured metals, after melting at the crucible, by the projection of

You do not reduce (i) the substances, if you do not dissolve them, if you do not exhaust them from their liquid part (2 ), you will do nothing. Let us now come to the speeches of the writer; let us listen to what he says (3). First, there is the rhubarb of the bridge. Note the circumspection of our author. He began with the plants, in order to indicate the flower; for the plants bear flowers. He spoke of the rhubarb of the Bridge, because the Pont-Euxin (5) is fed by the rivers that flow there. Therefore, wanting to bring this point to light, it means by this (6) depletion of the liquid part, darkening (7) and attenuation (8) of metal bodies, or substances. 3 bis. Dioscorus. And in what sense does he say: ‘ the oath has been imposed on us not to expose anything clearly to anyone’?
Synesius.
He rightly said “to no one,” that is to say, to no one among the uninitiated. The word person does not refer to everyone absolutely; for he himself speaks for those who are initiated and who have
Practised mind.

certain materials, and metals colored by way of coating. The coating could also constitute a simple superficial varnish; or else attack the metal, forming on its surface an alloy, amalgam, sulfide, or arsenide, the shade of which was moreover modifiable by the action of fire. (V. /ji/rOii. ,p. Sg and 60.)
(i) That is to say, bodies must be reduced to their last degree of division; to their quintessence, as was said later in the Middle Ages.

Sees here the idea of fixing bodies, by removing their liquidity, or fusibility; this quality being considered as a distinct element of bodies. (C'p.flrigines de l'Alchimie, p. 280 and 281.) (3) The obscure but positive recipes of the Pseudo-Democritus, which are those of an experimenter, follow the mystical commentaries of a Neo-Platonic philosopher.

(4) That is, the color, flos, Ilyaici a pun. (5) The Greek simply says: -';, the sea. There is another play of words whose meaning escapes us. Unless we interpret this sentence in figure 18 of the Introd. , p. 3. 141; in which is represented a vessel called '-, in the form of a basin, and in which flows the jet of a distillation, operated with the products here designated under the mystical name of flowers. (6) See note (2) above. (7) Oxidation or surface sulphuration which destroys the luster of the metal. The metals in fact lose their brilliance by oxidizing and changing into powdery materials, such as green-of-grey, rust, etc. (8) That is, the reduction to their last degree of division. See note (1) above.
Notice again what he says in the Introduction of the Chrjsopec: "mercury, coming from the cinnabar and the chrysocolle".
D. Do we need these kinds of (substances)?
5. No, Dioscorus.
D. But what do we need?
You heard it; hear it again.

In speaking of the dissolution of (metallic) bodies, it is meant that you dissolve them and make them waters (i); so that they become fluid and darkened (2) and are attenuated (3). This is what is called divine water (4), mercury, chrysocolla, apyrous sulfur. There are other denominations as well. Thus whitening is calcination, and yellowing is igneous regeneration; for such as these

They are the ones who heal themselves, and they are the ones who heal themselves. But the Philosopher has designated them by several names (6) and sometimes in the singular, sometimes in the plural, in order to exercise us and see if we are intelligent; for he said, continuing his discourse: “If you are intelligent and proceed as it has been written, you will be happy; for you will overcome by the method poverty, this incurable evil.” He therefore turns us away and detaches us from vain error, in order to free us from this imagination of the plurality of materials.
(i) Liquids.
(2) See note (7) on the previous page.
(3) "See note (i) on the previous page.
(4) Or sulphur water.

In other words, to achieve these effects, metals must be attacked with the help of divine water, mercury, chrysocolla, and sulfur. The Greek phrase is elliptical. In asserting that these substances are not needed, the author seems to mean that these agents do not experience transmutation by themselves: they are not the fundamental matter, but the intermediaries.

(5) Is this to be understood as pyrites which, once heated, burn, roast and change into oxides, without external fuel? And sulphides, which can regenerate their metals by a controlled mesh, such as lead sulphides, antimony, etc.? (6) On this multiplicity of mystical names, intended to veil science from the uninitiated, see the prophetic nomenclature, Introd. , p. 3. 10. These names, moreover, do not necessarily apply to the same substance; but they sometimes designate the different substances employed in the sequence of the same operation. (7) See I, XV, p. 37 of this volume.

Pay attention to what he says in the Introduction to his book: “I also come to Egypt, bringing natural questions, so that you may disdain multiple matter” (i). It is called solid (metallic) bodies. For if these (bodies) are not dissolved and then solidified again, nothing will come to pass for the accomplishment of the work. 5. In order that we may understand that liquids are derived from solidsin other words, the flowersee how it expresses itself: “The products contained in liquors are the saffron of Cilicia, Taristoloche, etc.

Thus speaking of the heads, He has shown us that the waters flow from the solids. And to persuade us that this is so, after saying "the urine of an impubère", he adds: "the water of lime, the water of cabbage ash, the water of lees, the water of alum"; and, in the end, he speaks of dog's milk. It is evident to us that this is taken in the vulgar sense; for he has introduced as substances suitable for dissolving (metallic) bodies, natron water and leech water. See how he said: "The very object of Chrysopaea is the things that transform matter and produce metals (?) and the

(substances) that resist the action of fire; for outside these things there is nothing certain. If, then, you are wise and proceed as it was written, you will be blessed.” 6. And how should I understand? Philosopher, I want to learn from you the method. For if I refer only to the explanations given (previously), I shall not profit from them. 5. Listen, Dioscorus, how he speaks; sharpen your mind on the text of his speech, and apply yourself (to grasp) in what sense he says: “Transform their nature, for nature has been hidden within” (4).
Synesius, what transformation is he talking about?
Of that of the bodies (metallic.)
(i) The Greek text of Democritus given words above is a little diflërent (v.
(4) Is this the regeneration of the Greek text and p. 44 of Trades Metals, latent in their mineralization).
Rais? or the manufacture of alloys
(2) The coloring principle provided by a dissolution (v. Flos, Floridiis.
variously colored and that it is necessary to dye, not only on the surface, but in the depth?
(3) The author plays on the similarity
And how to accomplish it, how to transport nature to the outside?
Sharpen your mind, Dioscorus, and pay attention to the expressions used.
D. How does it express itself?

So if you treat (the matter) properly, you transport nature outside. It is the land of Chio, the asterite, the white cadmie, etc. Note what the circumspection of the author is, how he alluded to all kinds of white substances, in order to make the whitening heard. So what he says, Dioscorus, is this: Put the (metallic) bodies with the mercury and divide finely, and then take another mercury. Mercury attracts all things to itself. Let macerate 3 or days throws the product in; botarion

(matras or digestion vessel), and place on an ash bath which is not heated by a burning fire, but gently heated; that is, on a keratokis bath. During the action of the fire, a glass instrument in the form of a lamella, adapted to its upper part, with capital (i), is adjusted to the botarion. Receive the water that escapes through the tip of the throat and keep it for decomposition: this is called divine water (or sulfur water). It produces transformation, that is, the operation that brings hidden nature to the outside: this is called the dissolution of bodies.

(metallic). This (preparation), when it has been broken down, takes the name of vinegar, or aminean wine, and similar names. In order that you may admire the skill of the author, see how he formed two catalogues: [one] of Chrysopea, (the other) of Argyropea, and besides two liquids: one for yellow, the other for white, that is, for gold and silver; he named the catalogue of gold, Chrysopea, and that of Argyropea.
You speak quite well, philosopher Synesius. But what
(i) This description is that of a still, with a water bath and a condensing flask (v. fig. 40, Introd. , p. 3. 164.
These are the two chapters of "Natural and Mysterious Questions," p. 45 and p. 52.

is the first point of art, is it bleaching, or yellowing? S. It's more like bleaching. D. And why is he talking about yellowing first? S. Because gold is preferred to silver. D. Do we have to do this, Synesius? S. No, Dioscorus; but it is proper to exercise our mind and thought. This is how things were arranged. Listen to him speak: “I talk to you as intelligent people, and I exercise your mind. Now, if you want to know exactly, be careful that in both catalogs mercury has been classified before all things, and in yellow: which means gold; and in white: which means silver. Dancing
(The treatise of) gold, it says, "Mercury which comes from the cinnabar." And in the (treaty of) white, it is said: "mercury that comes from arsenic or beyond sandarachus (i)", etc.
8. Is mercury of different kinds?
S. Yes, it is of different kinds, while being one.
D. But, if it is one, how is it of different kinds?
Yes, it is of different kinds, and it has a very great power.
Didn't you hear Hermes say, "The honeycomb (2) is white," and

“The honeycomb is yellow.” D. Yes, I (he) heard it. But what I want to learn, Synesius, teach me: this is the operation you know. Does mercury take on the appearance of all bodies anyway? S. You got it, Dioscorus. In fact, just as wax affects the color it receives; just as mercury, O philosopher, whitens all bodies and attracts their souls; it digests them by cooking and seizes them. This shows that the word mercury meant both our mercury and ours is about the tinctorial action that arsenic, as well as ordinary mercury, can exert on metals. Hence the idea of an essence common to the two agents. It seems that the observations relating to these two bodies were the starting point of the philosophers' notion of mercury, or metallic raw material, intended to be the intermediary of transmutation. (2) That is, mercury.

Even the principle of all liquidity, when it has undergone decomposition, it operates everywhere the change of colors. It forms the permanent background (i), while the colors have no foundation of their own. Or rather, mercury, losing its own foundation, becomes a subject that can be modified by the treatments carried out on metal bodies and their materials (2).
9. And what are these bodies and their materials (3)?
It is tetrasomy (4) and its congeners.
D. And what are his congeners?
S. You have heard that their matter is their soul (5).
D. So the materials (metals) are their souls?

Yes; for just as the carpenter, when he takes an object of wood and makes a seat, or a chariot, or something else, works only on matter; so too does this art, O philosopher, when it divides bodies. Listen, Dioscorus: the stonemason cuts the stone, or the saw, to make it fit for his use. Similarly also the carpenter saws and prunes the wood, to make it a seat, or a chariot: Tartiste does not thereby seek to modify anything other than the form; for there is nothing there but wood.
